chapters.title: The Transformation Thesis: From Chronic Diluter to Self-Funded Compounder
chapters.body:
In May 2026, Coeur Mining carried a market capitalisation of approximately $18.8 billion — a figure so remote from the company's recent past that it requires a deliberate act of historical imagination to process. Less than three years earlier, CDE shares traded in a $4–5 range as the Rochester heap-leach expansion consumed capital faster than the mine could generate it, and analysts debated whether management had mortgaged the balance sheet beyond recovery. That the stock had since reached roughly $18.34, implying a re-rating of more than 3.5 times over eighteen months, is the central fact this dossier interrogates. The question is whether the re-rating reflects durable operational transformation — or a precious-metals bull market that has temporarily papered over the execution risks embedded in one of the most aggressive acquisition programmes in recent North American mining history.

## Three Arcs, One Thesis

The Coeur of May 2026 is the product of three overlapping strategic arcs executed in compressed succession. The first was operational rehabilitation: the $730 million Plan of Operations Amendment 11 expansion at Rochester in Nevada, completed in March 2024, took an undercapitalised heap-leach operation and rebuilt it from the pad up into one of the largest silver-gold processing complexes in the United States, targeting 32 million tonnes of annual ore throughput. The second arc was inorganic silver growth: the February 2025 all-stock acquisition of SilverCrest Metals and its Las Chispas underground mine in Sonora, Mexico, added what management described as one of the world's lowest-cost, highest-grade silver-gold operations to a portfolio that had long needed a flagship. The third arc — and by far the most consequential in scale — was the March 2026 completion of the approximately $7 billion all-stock acquisition of New Gold Inc., which brought the Rainy River open-pit and underground mine in northwestern Ontario and the New Afton block-cave near Kamloops, British Columbia, into the consolidated group. Together, the three arcs transformed a five-mine, predominantly US-and-Mexico operator into a seven-mine North American conglomerate spanning Mexico, Nevada, Alaska, South Dakota, British Columbia, and Ontario.

## Scale and Revenue

The financial signature of that transformation is visible in a single quarterly number. In the first quarter of 2026, Coeur reported consolidated revenue of [$856 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000215466/000021546626000021/a1q26earningsreleaseex-991.htm) — a figure that included only eleven days of New Gold contribution following the March 20 closing date. Adjusted EBITDA for the quarter reached $475 million. Those results arrived against a commodity backdrop that management's full-year 2026 guidance formalised as gold at $4,550 per ounce and silver at $77.50 per ounce; on those assumptions, the company guided to approximately $3 billion of consolidated adjusted EBITDA and roughly $2 billion of free cash flow for the full year. As a point of reference, Coeur's entire 2023 revenue base was approximately $510 million.

| Period | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA | Free Cash Flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | ~$510 M | — | — |
| FY 2024 | $1.1 B | $339 M | ($9 M) |
| FY 2025 | $2.1 B | $1.0 B | $666 M |
| Q1 2026 | $856 M | $475 M | — |
| FY 2026 guided | ~$3.4 B (annualised) | ~$3 B | ~$2 B |

## Mitchell Krebs and the Durability Question

Presiding over each phase of this evolution is Mitchell J. Krebs, who has served as President and Chief Executive Officer since 2011 — a fifteen-year tenure that spans the silver price collapse of 2013–2016, the balance-sheet rehabilitation that followed, the Rochester capital commitment, and now two transformative acquisitions inside fourteen months. Krebs came to the chief executive role from the company's corporate development function, where he had worked since joining from investment banking in New York in 1995; his background is transactional, and the strategic record reflects it. The Rochester ramp and the rapid Las Chispas integration, which brought Las Chispas adjusted costs to $10.75 per silver ounce in the third quarter of 2025 in its first full period of Coeur ownership, earned him credibility with an investor base that had grown accustomed to disappointment.

But the dossier question is forward-looking in the sense that matters: can the capital discipline forged during the Rochester ramp and Las Chispas integration survive contact with an integration far more complex in geography, metallurgy, and organisational scale? Coeur's share count stands at approximately 1.03 billion following the New Gold closing — more than 2.5 times the roughly 399 million shares outstanding at the end of 2024. That dilution is the tax the company paid for growth without debt; the implicit contract with shareholders is that per-share cash flows will compound fast enough to justify it. The inaugural semi-annual cash dividend of $0.02 per share declared in May 2026 was a symbolic marker of that intent. Whether it proves the beginning of a sustained return programme or a premature signal of confidence will depend on execution that has not yet been fully demonstrated.

chapters.title: From Idaho Silver Camp to Chicago Boardroom: Ninety-Seven Years of Strategic Reinvention
chapters.body:
## Silver in the Dirt: 1928–1980

The story of Coeur Mining begins in the spring of 1928, in a stretch of rugged terrain straddling the Idaho-Montana border where silver had been pulled from the earth since the 1880s. The Coeur d'Alene mining district — named for the indigenous people who had fished its lake and hunted its forests for generations — had by then become one of the most productive silver regions on the planet, home to storied operations like the Bunker Hill, the Sunshine, and the Lucky Friday. Into this crowded and deeply competitive landscape, Coeur d'Alene Mines Corporation was incorporated: a modest regional enterprise that would spend its first half-century doing what every other company in the district did — drilling, blasting, and hauling silver from the narrow veins that threaded through the Precambrian rock beneath northern Idaho.

For the next five decades, Coeur d'Alene Mines remained exactly what its name advertised. Production volumes varied with the price of silver, which itself oscillated dramatically through the Depression, the Second World War, and the postwar industrial boom. The company survived these cycles by virtue of the same attributes that defined the district itself: low extraction costs, rich grades, and the modest balance-sheet requirements of a single-geography, single-commodity producer. Capital came primarily from retained cash flow; debt was regarded with suspicion. It was a posture that, for reasons the company's leadership would not fully appreciate until much later, stored up enormous strategic risk — a narrow base ill-suited to surviving a prolonged price dislocation.

## The Diversification Years: 1983–2007

The first signal that the company's geographic ambitions exceeded its Idaho origins came in 1983, when Coeur d'Alene Mines acquired an operating lease on the Rochester silver-gold mine in Pershing County, Nevada. A large-footprint, low-grade heap-leach operation, Rochester contrasted sharply with the narrow underground mines of the home district but offered material scale at modest capital intensity. The following year, in 1984, the company purchased the Wharf gold mine outright in Lawrence County, South Dakota, establishing a presence in the Black Hills and effectively declaring itself a multi-state precious-metals company. An initial interest in the Kensington gold property near Juneau, Alaska, followed in 1987, planting a flag in Southeast Alaska that would yield a long-lived underground gold mine but would also consume capital for years before reaching production.

The 1990s inaugurated an era of genuinely international ambition. Chile came first, with the acquisition of the Fachinal and Cerro Bayo projects in 1990 — high-altitude, high-grade silver assets that extended the portfolio into the Andes. Bolivia followed in 1999 with the San Bartolomé silver project, a large heap-leach operation near Potosí intended as a cornerstone of the Latin American strategy. Argentina entered the portfolio in 2002 with the Martha mine, a narrow-vein underground silver producer in Santa Cruz Province. Mexico arrived in 2007 with the Palmarejo silver-gold project in Chihuahua, acquired in a transaction that added high-grade underground operations and a long mine life — but also a legacy gold streaming agreement with Franco-Nevada that would cast a long shadow over subsequent financials.

The strategic logic was consistent if not always rigorous: silver is silver wherever it sits in the ground, and diversification across jurisdictions ostensibly reduced the single-country risks that had periodically disrupted Idaho production. The Latin American expansion also offered higher-grade, lower-cost ounces intended to subsidise the capital demands of the North American portfolio. Not all of these ventures survived. Fachinal in Chile was eventually sold. The Martha mine in Argentina was wound down. Most consequentially, San Bartolomé — the Bolivian project that had once seemed central to the company's identity — would ultimately be divested in 2018, sold to Andean Precious Metals for proceeds that helped patch a badly damaged balance sheet. The divestiture was an acknowledgement that sovereign risk in Bolivia, acceptable when the company was growing, had become unaffordable when it was fighting for survival.

What survived from the international expansion era was Palmarejo in Chihuahua — and it survived encumbered. The Franco-Nevada streaming agreement, under which approximately 40–50 percent of Palmarejo's annual gold production is delivered at a fixed price of $800 per ounce, had been a reasonable financing mechanism at the time of the original transaction. By the mid-2020s, with gold trading above $4,000 per ounce, those terms had become a structural drag on the mine's margin — a permanent reminder that the price at which capital was raised in a prior cycle governs the economics of the asset in all subsequent cycles.

## Chicago, 2013: A Rebrand as Corporate Signal

By 2013, Coeur d'Alene Mines Corporation had become an awkward artifact of its own history. The name still pointed to a silver camp in northern Idaho; the operating reality was a multi-country portfolio with shareholders who traded the stock in New York. The decision to rename the company Coeur Mining, Inc. and relocate its corporate headquarters from Coeur d'Alene to Chicago was a deliberate act of corporate repositioning — a statement to institutional investors that management regarded itself as running a professionally managed diversified precious-metals producer, not a regional miner that had grown beyond its bounds.

The Chicago address placed the company in the orbit of Midwestern institutional capital and a major financial centre, signalling a governance ambition the Idaho office had made harder to project. Mitchell Krebs, who had been appointed president and chief executive in 2011 after joining the company as an investment banker-turned-corporate development executive in 1995, oversaw the rebrand. His background — economics at the Wharton School, an MBA from Harvard Business School, years of corporate development inside the company — fitted precisely the professional management profile the new identity was designed to embody.

## The Near-Death Experience: 2015–2016

Whatever strategic progress the rebranding represented, it could not insulate Coeur Mining from the catastrophic silver price decline that began in 2013 and reached its nadir in late 2015 and early 2016. Silver, which had briefly touched nearly $50 per ounce in April 2011, fell below $14 per ounce in late 2015. For a company carrying meaningful debt across a portfolio of mines whose economics had been underwritten at higher price assumptions, the consequences were severe.

The balance sheet deteriorated rapidly. Equity offerings diluted existing shareholders; debt covenants came under pressure. The company found itself in the uncomfortable position of generating inadequate free cash flow to service obligations while simultaneously needing to allocate capital to maintain operations and advance development projects. San Bartolomé's eventual divestiture in 2018 was a direct consequence of this period — an acknowledgement that a geopolitically sensitive Bolivian asset was a liability in a capital-constrained environment that Coeur could no longer afford to carry.

The share count became the ledger of this distress. Equity issuances required to preserve the balance sheet pushed the outstanding count materially higher through the late 2010s, establishing a dilution baseline that would only accelerate with the Rochester expansion and the all-stock acquisition programme of 2024–2026. By year-end 2024, shares outstanding stood at approximately 399 million — already substantially above pre-crisis levels, already reflecting years of growth-by-dilution.

## Rochester, SilverCrest, and the Strategic Arc

The Rochester Plan of Operations Amendment 11 expansion — a $730 million capital programme to more than double the Nevada mine's throughput to 32 million tonnes per year — was the first major test of Krebs's post-crisis capital discipline doctrine. Approved and funded across 2021–2024, the project required additional share issuances and incremental debt during a period when silver prices remained volatile. Rochester achieved commercial production on March 31, 2024 and, by year-end 2025, had delivered 6.1 million silver ounces for the full year at record quarterly throughput rates.

The SilverCrest acquisition, announced in October 2024 at an implied equity value of approximately $1.7 billion in an all-stock transaction, added the Las Chispas mine in Sonora — one of the world's highest-grade, lowest-cost silver operations — with SilverCrest shareholders receiving 1.6022 Coeur shares per share held. The deal closed in February 2025 following Mexican antitrust clearance from COFECE. The New Gold transaction, announced in November 2025 at an implied value of approximately $7 billion and closed on March 20, 2026, then added the Rainy River and New Afton operations in Ontario and British Columbia.

The share count arithmetic is unsparing. The approximately 1.03 billion shares outstanding after the New Gold close represented an increase of more than 2.5 times the pre-SilverCrest level of 399 million at year-end 2024. Whether those shares represent the foundation of a genuinely transformed large-cap precious-metals company — with seven mines, $856 million of quarterly revenue, and the capacity to generate $2 billion of annual free cash flow at current spot prices — or the accumulated cost of an acquisition programme that outpaced the organic value creation it was meant to amplify is a question the coming years of operational execution will answer. Ninety-seven years after the company was incorporated to exploit a silver camp in northern Idaho, the answer remains open.

chapters.title: Seven Mines, Three Countries: The Architecture of the Operating Portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Portfolio in Full

By the time Coeur Mining closed the New Gold transaction on March 20, 2026, Mitchell Krebs had assembled a seven-mine operating portfolio spanning three countries, five jurisdictions, and four distinct mining methods — a configuration with no precedent in the company's ninety-seven-year history. The architecture is not tidy. It ranges from one of the world's most cost-efficient narrow-vein underground mines in the Sonoran desert to a technically demanding block-cave operation in the interior of British Columbia. Taken together, the portfolio produced 419,046 gold ounces and 17.9 million silver ounces in fiscal year 2025 across the legacy five mines, before the Canadian assets contributed so much as a single shift of reportable production. What follows is a mine-by-mine account of what Coeur actually owns.

## Las Chispas: The Crown Jewel

Las Chispas sits in Arizpe Municipality in the state of Sonora, Mexico — a narrow-vein underground silver-gold mine that SilverCrest Metals developed from discovery to commercial production in fewer than five years at a capital cost of roughly $220 million. Coeur acquired it in February 2025 as part of the $1.7 billion all-stock SilverCrest transaction, and it immediately reset the portfolio's cost profile.

The structural reasons for Las Chispas's cost advantage begin underground. Narrow-vein deposits of the type mined at Las Chispas — where individual veins carry grades that can exceed 1,000 grams per tonne silver equivalent — allow an operator to process a relatively small tonne throughput while delivering disproportionate metal output. There is no need for a massive grinding circuit or a large-footprint leach pad. The mine fleet is compact, the haul distances short, and the processing plant modest in scale. These physical characteristics translate directly into lower energy consumption, lower reagent use, lower labour per ounce, and lower sustaining capital per unit of production compared with bulk open-pit or heap-leach operations.

In the six weeks following the February 2025 close, Las Chispas contributed 714,239 silver ounces and 7,175 gold ounces at an adjusted cost applicable to sales of just $8.38 per silver ounce — a figure that understated normalised operating costs because it excluded certain ramp-up adjustments but nonetheless signalled the asset's structural positioning. By the third quarter of 2025, with a full quarter of Coeur ownership embedded, adjusted CAS had settled at $10.75 per silver ounce. The full-year 2025 figure of $19.11 per silver ounce reflects certain inventory timing effects and the partial-year contribution from the February close; the underlying mine-level economics remained among the lowest of any silver producer in North America. Coeur's 2026 guidance for Las Chispas projects 5.5–6.3 million silver ounces and 55,000–65,000 gold ounces, anchoring the portfolio's silver production envelope at unit costs the legacy Coeur assets cannot approach.

## Palmarejo and the Franco-Nevada Constraint

Palmarejo, a long-running underground silver-gold mine in the sierra of Chihuahua, Mexico, has been part of Coeur's portfolio since a 2007 acquisition. It is a mature asset with mechanised cut-and-fill mining, a conventional milling circuit, and a history of steady production — but it carries a structural financial overhang that has defined its economics for more than a decade.

Under a gold streaming agreement with Franco-Nevada Corporation, Palmarejo delivers approximately 40 to 50 percent of its annual gold production at a fixed price of $800 per ounce. With gold trading near $4,550 per ounce in Coeur's 2026 guidance assumptions, each ounce delivered under the stream represents a realised price roughly $3,750 below spot — a discount that flows directly to Franco-Nevada as economic value transferred. The agreement was negotiated in 2009 when Palmarejo was still under development and Coeur's balance sheet required structured financing; the cost of that capital, in hindsight, has been paid many times over in foregone gold revenue. Adjusted CAS at Palmarejo registered $871 per gold ounce in 2025, competitive in isolation but materially constrained in net realisation terms by the streaming obligation.

Coeur has responded by expanding exploration activity in areas of the Palmarejo district that fall outside the stream's geographic scope, attempting to accumulate a production base from which the Franco-Nevada entitlement represents a shrinking proportionate burden. Whether that strategy succeeds depends on drill results that, at the frozen snapshot date, remained a work in progress.

## Rochester: Capital Made Real

Rochester, in Pershing County, Nevada, is the portfolio's most consequential capital story. Coeur acquired an operating lease on the Rochester silver-gold heap-leach deposit in 1983 and has mined it continuously — more than four decades of open-pit production in the high desert. The POA 11 expansion, approved in 2020 and completed at a cost of approximately $730 million, was the largest capital project in the company's history and the defining financial commitment of the Krebs era.

The investment funded a second crushing circuit designed to increase ore throughput to 32 million tonnes per year, one of the world's largest Merrill-Crowe precious-metals recovery facilities, and a new Stage 6 leach pad extending reserve capacity across an enlarged footprint. Commercial production was declared on March 31, 2024. In the first full year of expanded operations, Rochester produced 6.1 million silver ounces and 60,178 gold ounces — production volumes that, in isolation, would qualify as a standalone mid-tier silver mine.

The cost structure reflects the economics of bulk heap-leach processing. Full-year 2025 adjusted CAS of $18.39 per silver ounce is approximately 70 percent higher than Las Chispas's realised cost in the same period. The structural explanation is straightforward: Rochester processes ore grading in the low single digits of grams per tonne silver equivalent, versus the triple-digit grades achievable in the best Las Chispas veins. Heap-leach recovery rates are inherently lower than conventional milling, and the process is slow — metal that enters a leach pad may not be recovered and reported for months. Operating leverage at Rochester runs through tonnes, not grade: the thesis is that processing vast quantities of low-grade material at high throughput rates generates acceptable absolute costs per ounce even if the unit rate cannot match a narrow-vein underground mine. As Rochester approaches its 32 million tonne throughput target, the economics should improve further; the 2025 performance represents a mine still in ramp-up, not steady-state operation.

## Kensington and Wharf: The Steady Producers

Kensington, an underground gold mine near Juneau in southeastern Alaska, is Coeur's most reliable gold producer — a long-life, mechanised operation that generated approximately 100,000 to 110,000 gold ounces annually across the recent production history at an adjusted CAS of $1,685 per gold ounce in 2025. The mine operates in a challenging maritime environment, with all supplies barged or flown to a remote site, contributing to unit costs that, while not exceptional, are supported by high-grade ore from multiple underground zones. Kensington provides operational continuity and Alaskan jurisdiction exposure in a portfolio otherwise weighted toward Mexico and Canada.

Wharf, in the Black Hills of Lawrence County, South Dakota, is the portfolio's most straightforward asset: a surface gold mine using conventional truck-and-shovel open-pit methods and heap-leach processing in a well-established mining district. Adjusted CAS at Wharf registered $1,151 per gold ounce in 2025. A reserve restatement during the year approximately doubled the declared mineral reserve base, extending mine life to roughly twelve years — a significant life extension for an asset that had periodically appeared at risk of depletion. Wharf requires modest sustaining capital and generates predictable free cash flow, functioning as the portfolio's low-volatility backstop.

## The Canadian Additions: Rainy River and New Afton

The March 2026 New Gold close added two Canadian operations whose full contribution to Coeur's consolidated results will not appear in audited form until the fiscal year 2026 annual report. At the frozen snapshot date, only eleven days of Q1 2026 production data — 14,145 gold ounces across both assets — had been incorporated into Coeur's reported financials.

Rainy River is an open-pit and underground gold-silver mine in northwestern Ontario. Under New Gold's ownership the project endured repeated capital overruns and mine-plan revisions after its 2017 commissioning, episodes that eroded New Gold's balance sheet and contributed to its strategic vulnerability. Coeur's 2026 guidance assumes Rainy River contributes within a combined Canadian envelope of 430,000–480,000 gold ounces and 50–65 million copper pounds, shared with New Afton.

New Afton, near Kamloops in British Columbia, operates as a block-cave gold-copper mine — the most technically demanding mining method in commercial use, in which an entire ore column is undercut and allowed to collapse under its own weight into a series of draw-points. The mine produces both gold and copper concentrate, adding a commodity exposure Coeur had not previously carried. The key future value driver at New Afton is the K-Zone resource, located below the current B-Cave operations and containing an estimated 47.6 million tonnes grading sufficient to support 715,000 ounces of gold and 606 million pounds of copper. Developing the K-Zone requires underground capital investment and technically demanding geomechanical execution, but represents one of the largest single sources of embedded value in Coeur's expanded portfolio.

## Silvertip: The Long Option

Silvertip, a zinc-lead-silver polymetallic deposit in northern British Columbia, sits outside Coeur's producing asset base entirely. The project was placed on care and maintenance in 2020 following a resource update, and remained non-producing at the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026. Its value is optionality: a high-grade underground deposit in a stable Canadian jurisdiction, held at low carrying cost, whose development decision will be made when zinc and lead market conditions, capital availability, and Coeur's integration priorities permit. In a portfolio now anchored by precious metals cash generation, Silvertip represents a distinct commodity profile and a future capital call that management has not yet elected to make.

chapters.title: The Numbers Behind the Re-Rating: Revenue Inflection, Margin Expansion, and the Dilution Trade-Off
chapters.body:
## Revenue Inflection: A Four-Year Quadrupling

The financial history of Coeur Mining between 2022 and 2026 is, in the most clinical sense, a table that should not exist. A company that recorded approximately $510 million in revenue in 2023 — the year its Rochester expansion consumed its last large tranche of capital and its balance sheet bent toward distress — reported $2.1 billion in revenue just two years later, and $856 million in a single quarter by early 2026. The sequence defies the conventional arc of mid-tier mining rehabilitation, which typically requires a decade of incremental improvement. Coeur compressed it into roughly twenty-four months.

| Fiscal Year / Period | Revenue | Adjusted EBITDA | Net Income | Free Cash Flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2023 | ~$510 million | — | — | — |
| FY 2024 | $1.1 billion | $339 million | $59 million | -$9 million |
| FY 2025 | $2.1 billion | $1.0 billion | $586 million | $666 million |
| Q1 2026 | $856 million | $475 million | — | — |

Each step-change in that table has a discrete mechanical explanation. The 2024 revenue more than doubled 2023's tally primarily because Rochester's POA 11 expansion — commissioned at commercial production on March 31, 2024 — began delivering the throughput its $730 million capital programme had been designed to produce. Silver and gold volumes from Rochester climbed sharply through the year as the new Merrill-Crowe plant and Stage 6 leach pad moved from commissioning toward steady-state operation. The 2025 number reflects two compounding forces: a full year of Rochester at elevated throughput, and the February 2025 addition of Las Chispas, the high-grade Sonoran silver-gold underground mine acquired via the all-stock SilverCrest transaction, which contributed 714,239 silver ounces in its initial six-week Q1 2025 alone. The $856 million reported for Q1 2026 is arithmetically startling but analytically coherent: it reflects the legacy five-mine portfolio operating at peak throughput and near-record realised prices, plus eleven days of New Gold contribution following the March 20, 2026 close. Annualised, Q1 2026 implies a revenue run rate comfortably above $3.4 billion once Rainy River and New Afton are included for full quarters.

## Margin Architecture: Where the EBITDA Is Made

The $1.0 billion of adjusted EBITDA Coeur reported for fiscal year 2025 was not evenly distributed. Las Chispas, operating as a narrow-vein underground mine with adjusted costs running near $10–19 per silver ounce — against a realised silver price that averaged well above $30 per ounce for most of 2025 — carried by far the portfolio's best margin, with an adjusted EBITDA margin approaching 70 percent. The asset is structurally exceptional: high-grade ore averaging well above 600 grams per tonne silver-equivalent, short haulage distances, and a pre-existing infrastructure footprint that SilverCrest built to a high specification before the acquisition.

Palmarejo, the company's longest-held Mexican asset, is a mid-to-high margin contributor on a gross basis, with adjusted costs per gold-equivalent ounce in the $871/oz range — materially lower than its peer-group average. Rochester's 2025 adjusted cost of $18.39 per silver ounce, while representing a significant improvement over the construction-phase years, still places it in the mid-tier of heap-leach operators globally. The mine's margins are improving with throughput leverage — fixed costs spread across more tonnes — but remain below Las Chispas and Palmarejo on a percentage basis. Kensington, Coeur's underground gold mine near Juneau, Alaska, is the portfolio's margin laggard, with adjusted costs of $1,685 per gold ounce reflecting Alaska's structural cost premiums — logistics, labour, and power — that no amount of operational optimisation fully offsets. Wharf, the open-pit heap-leach gold mine in South Dakota's Black Hills, sits in the mid-tier at $1,151 per gold ounce and benefits from low capital intensity; its reserve life extension to approximately twelve years, following a 2025 restatement that doubled the reported mineral reserve base, meaningfully improved its contribution to the portfolio's medium-term cash generation profile.

## The Franco-Nevada Discount: A Structural Revenue Haircut

No analysis of Coeur's margin architecture is complete without quantifying the Franco-Nevada gold stream at Palmarejo, which represents the single most significant recurring headwind on the income statement. Under the legacy streaming agreement, Franco-Nevada receives approximately 40 to 50 percent of Palmarejo's annual gold production at a fixed delivery price of $800 per ounce. In a world where Coeur's 2026 guidance assumes a gold realisation of $4,550 per ounce, that fixed price implies a forgone revenue figure of approximately $3,750 for every ounce delivered into the stream.

Palmarejo produced 100,768 gold ounces in fiscal year 2025. Applying the 40-to-50-percent streaming obligation range implies 40,307 to 50,384 ounces delivered to Franco-Nevada at the below-market fixed price in 2025 alone — translating to between $151 million and $189 million of forgone revenue at 2026-equivalent gold price assumptions. Over a full cycle, the stream is not merely a royalty rate; it is a structurally embedded cost that permanently reduces Palmarejo's contribution margin relative to an unencumbered asset. Management has acknowledged the stream as a legacy burden — negotiated in 2009 when Coeur was a smaller, capital-constrained operator — but has made no indication of willingness or ability to renegotiate its terms. The stream is, in effect, a perpetual tax on Palmarejo's gold production, and analysts modelling the mine's standalone value should apply a meaningful discount to the portion of gold output it encumbers.

## Capital Expenditure: From Inferno to Normalisation

The capex history at Coeur is the backstory behind the revenue table. Between 2021 and 2024, the Rochester POA 11 expansion absorbed approximately $730 million in cumulative capital — more than the company's entire annual revenue in 2023. That investment crowded out nearly everything else: share issuances were required to fund the gap between operating cash flow and construction outflows, debt balances swelled, and the share price languished in the $4–5 range as the market priced in meaningful execution risk.

| Period | Capital Expenditure | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 2021–2024 (cumulative) | ~$730 million | Rochester POA 11 expansion |
| FY 2025 | $221 million | Post-construction normalisation |
| FY 2026 (guidance) | $305–364 million | Includes New Gold sustaining + development capital |
| Exploration (2026) | $120–136 million | Including Silvertip and New Gold brownfield |

The step from $221 million in 2025 to $305–364 million in 2026 reflects the addition of New Gold's sustaining and development capital requirements at Rainy River and New Afton. New Afton's K-Zone resource extension, if pursued, will require continued underground development capital; Rainy River carries its own sustaining programme as a conventional open-pit and underground operation. Relative to Rochester's construction peak, however, even the 2026 combined figure represents a fundamentally different capital intensity regime — one in which cash generation well exceeds investment requirements and free cash flow is available for debt service, taxes, and, for the first time in the company's recent history, shareholder distributions.

## The Capital Structure Paradox: Net Cash, 2.6x Dilution

Coeur ended fiscal year 2025 with total debt of $341 million against cash of $554 million — a net cash position of approximately $213 million, a figure that would have seemed implausible to any analyst covering the company during the Rochester construction years, when total debt exceeded $590 million at year-end 2024 and leverage ratios pressed toward 1.7x EBITDA. The $249 million of debt repaid during fiscal year 2025 was funded almost entirely by the $666 million free cash flow surge that Rochester's throughput ramp and Las Chispas margins jointly produced.

The asterisk on that balance sheet achievement is equity dilution of historic proportions. Shares outstanding stood at approximately 399 million at year-end 2024. The SilverCrest transaction, closed in February 2025 at an exchange ratio of 1.6022 Coeur shares per SilverCrest share, pushed the count to approximately 642 million. The New Gold acquisition — 0.4959 Coeur shares per New Gold share in a deal valued at approximately $7 billion — carried the total to approximately 1.03 billion shares by March 2026, a 2.6x expansion over eighteen months.

| Date | Shares Outstanding | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Year-end 2024 | ~399 million | Pre-SilverCrest baseline |
| February 2025 | ~642 million | SilverCrest close |
| March 2026 | ~1.03 billion | New Gold close |

The dilution is not inherently destructive — both acquisitions were paid in stock precisely because Coeur's equity had become the currency of its strategic ambition, and paying stock for assets that generate substantial free cash flow can be value-accretive if the acquired assets' per-share contribution exceeds the proportional claim of new shares issued. The test is whether the $3 billion EBITDA and $2 billion free cash flow guided for full-year 2026 will translate into per-share metrics that reward shareholders who held through the dilution.

## The Tax Cliff: $400–500 Million in Cash Obligations

The 2026 cash tax guidance of $400 to $500 million is the largest single-year cash tax obligation in Coeur's ninety-seven-year history, and it deserves more analytical attention than it typically receives in equity research coverage that focuses on adjusted metrics. The magnitude reflects the simultaneous profitability of operations across multiple high-tax jurisdictions: Mexico, where Palmarejo and Las Chispas are situated, applies a corporate income tax rate of 30 percent supplemented by a special mining duty; Canada, home to Rainy River and New Afton following the New Gold close, levies federal corporate tax at approximately 26.5 percent on mining income. Management's guided effective rate of 29 to 35 percent for 2026 implies that consolidated pre-tax income will approach $1.2 to $1.7 billion before tax — a figure consistent with the $3 billion EBITDA guidance after accounting for interest, depreciation, and development expense deductions. At the midpoint of the tax guidance, $450 million of cash taxes represents roughly 22 percent of the $2 billion free cash flow target, making it the largest single claim on cash generation after sustaining capital.

## Per-Share Economics: What the Dilution Bought

Coeur reported diluted earnings per share of $0.95 on a GAAP basis and $0.80 on an adjusted basis for fiscal year 2025, calculated on weighted-average diluted shares of 614.7 million — a share count that reflects partial-year SilverCrest dilution but not New Gold. Net income of $586 million on 614.7 million shares represents a substantial improvement over the $0.10 per share earned in 2024 on the pre-SilverCrest base.

The post-New Gold per-share arithmetic is more demanding. With approximately 1.03 billion shares outstanding following the March 2026 close and management guiding toward approximately $2 billion in free cash flow for full-year 2026, the implied free cash flow per share is approximately $1.94 — against a share price near $18.34 at the frozen snapshot date, a free cash flow yield of roughly 10.6 percent. That yield is generous by the standards of any capital-intensive industry, and it represents the market's current reward for investing through the Rochester construction, the balance-sheet stress of 2022–2024, and the dilution of two all-stock acquisitions. Whether the earnings per share trajectory justifies the 3.5x appreciation in the stock over eighteen months depends almost entirely on whether the $3 billion EBITDA guided for 2026 proves durable at the next turn of the precious-metals price cycle — a question the balance sheet, now net-cash and deleveraging, is at least structurally positioned to answer in the affirmative.

chapters.title: Eight Quarters of Evidence: The Quarterly Cadence from Rochester Ramp to Record Results
chapters.body:
## The Floor Beneath the Ramp

To appreciate how far Coeur Mining's quarterly earnings trajectory travelled between early 2024 and the spring of 2026, it helps to fix the starting point precisely. In the first quarter of 2024, the company's Rochester mine in Pershing County, Nevada — the asset that had absorbed $730 million of capital over three years — achieved commercial production on the very last day of the quarter, March 31. That timing meant the quarter contributed almost nothing from Rochester's expanded economics. With Las Chispas not yet in the portfolio and Palmarejo, Kensington, and Wharf running at their customary tempos, the company's first-quarter 2024 adjusted EBITDA hovered near $70 million, a figure that would have been quietly respectable for the old Coeur but now sat against a balance sheet carrying approximately $588 million of net debt.

The full-year 2024 tally — $339 million of adjusted EBITDA on revenue of $1.1 billion, with free cash flow barely negative at minus $9 million — reflected a company in transition rather than in momentum. Rochester was producing and placing ore on the Stage 6 leach pad at volumes that validated the engineering thesis but had not yet translated into the throughput economics that would justify the capital outlay. Net income was $59 million, modest for the scale of the enterprise. The quarters of 2024 traced a slow climb as Rochester's solutions production began to mature, but the decisive move awaited a catalyst from outside Nevada.

## The Las Chispas Quarter and Its Anomalies

That catalyst arrived in February 2025, when the SilverCrest transaction closed and Las Chispas entered Coeur's consolidation perimeter. The first quarter of 2025 is the most analytically complex in the eight-quarter sequence — it rewards careful disaggregation.

On the surface, Q1 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $149 million represented a 28 percent increase over the prior quarter. That advance is striking given that the quarter also absorbed approximately $130 million of one-time acquisition-related cash outlays associated with the SilverCrest transaction, including transaction costs and balance-sheet settlement items. Stripping those aside, the quarter's underlying operating delivery was substantially stronger.

Three components drove the outperformance. First, Las Chispas contributed roughly $72 million of EBITDA from inventory monetisation alone in its initial six-week reporting period — the mine had been operating continuously under SilverCrest before close and had accumulated refined and semi-processed inventory that crystallised as immediate cash upon acquisition. Second, Rochester seasonality worked in the company's favour: heap-leach operations in Nevada typically exhibit stronger precious-metals solution yields in Q1 as residual leach cycles from late-year ore placement mature. Third, Palmarejo's Franco-Nevada gold stream timing — the obligation to deliver approximately 40 to 50 percent of annual gold production at $800 per ounce — fell favourably within the quarter, amplifying realised gold margins on the portion outside the stream.

Mitchell Krebs, speaking on the Q1 2025 earnings call, kept his framing deliberately simple: the Las Chispas acquisition had 'proceeded smoothly,' a two-word assessment that masked the operational complexity of integrating a narrow-vein Mexican underground mine in a matter of weeks.

## Deleveraging as Strategy, Not Accident

The second and third quarters of 2025 established the company's free-cash-flow credentials — and management used them systematically to dismantle the balance sheet that had constrained strategic flexibility for years.

By the end of Q3 2025, Coeur had repaid in excess of $228 million of debt on a year-to-date basis, drawing down the revolving credit facility and retiring senior secured note balances at a pace that compressed the net leverage ratio from approximately 1.7 times at year-end 2024 to 0.1 times within nine months. CFO Thomas Whelan, who had been managing the balance-sheet arithmetic since the Rochester capital peak, described the deleveraging pace as a direct expression of the company's capital-allocation priority ordering: debt reduction first, then exploration reinvestment, then returns to shareholders — in that sequence.

Las Chispas continued to earn its acquisition price. In Q3 2025 — its second full quarter inside Coeur — the mine produced at adjusted costs of $10.75 per silver ounce, a level that placed it comfortably among the world's lowest-cost silver operations. Krebs, on the Q3 2025 call, noted that Las Chispas 'continues to exceed expectations in just its second full quarter,' a formulation that distinguished between the mine's standalone financial delivery and the integration execution overhead that Coeur's own organisation had managed. The distinction mattered: SilverCrest had run Las Chispas as a focused single-asset operator, and there was a plausible concern that embedding it within a multi-jurisdictional conglomerate would introduce cost creep. The Q3 data suggested the concern had not yet materialised.

## Three Consecutive Records

The fourth quarter of 2025 resolved any remaining ambiguity about the earnings trajectory. Adjusted EBITDA of $425 million for the quarter represented the highest quarterly result in the company's 97-year history, powered by Rochester throughput finally achieving the economics that had justified the POA 11 investment, Las Chispas running at its designed grade profile, and a gold price environment — spot gold had advanced to levels well above $2,500 per ounce by late 2025 — that amplified margins across every mine in the portfolio.

Rochester's specific contribution was notable. Krebs noted on the Q4 2025 earnings call that the mine's ore crushing and placement rates had reached 'record levels' in the quarter, a performance that validated the multi-year ramp narrative. Full-year 2025 Rochester production came in at 6.1 million silver ounces and 60,178 gold ounces at an adjusted cost of $18.39 per silver ounce — still above the long-term cost targets that management had articulated during the capital-raise years, but moving in the right direction as throughput economies began to compound.

The full-year 2025 picture, which Krebs characterised in the Q4 2025 call as 'record-setting financial results' accompanied by a 'third consecutive quarter of records,' showed the full dimension of the transformation: revenue of $2.1 billion, net income of $586 million, free cash flow of $666 million, and adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 billion. Against those same metrics in 2024 — $1.1 billion revenue, $59 million net income, negative $9 million free cash flow, $339 million EBITDA — the year-over-year change was less a financial improvement than a structural recomposition of the business.

## Q1 2026: The New Floor

The first quarter of 2026 added another record to the sequence even before the New Gold assets had been owned for a full quarter. The acquisition of New Gold closed on March 20, 2026 — eleven days before the end of Q1 — and the two Canadian mines contributed 14,145 gold ounces in that brief window. Despite that minimal contribution, Q1 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $475 million on revenue of $856 million exceeded the Q4 2025 record by approximately 12 percent, carried primarily by the five-mine legacy portfolio operating at what had by then become its steady-state economics.

The annualised implications were significant. A $475 million quarter, if sustained, implies roughly $1.9 billion of full-year EBITDA before any contribution from Rainy River or New Afton — two assets that, in full-quarter consolidation from Q2 2026 onward, would push management's guided EBITDA toward $3 billion for the full year.

## The Dividend as Narrative Close

In May 2026, Coeur's board declared the company's inaugural semi-annual cash dividend of $0.02 per share — a number too small, by any conventional yield analysis, to move the stock or attract income-oriented capital. Its significance lay elsewhere. For a company that had spent the better part of a decade in financial rehabilitation, issuing equity to fund a capital project and then further equity to make acquisitions, the act of declaring a dividend represented management's formal assertion that the free cash flow profile had become durable rather than episodic.

The eight quarters from Rochester's commercial production to that dividend declaration described a complete arc: capital absorption, operational proof, acquisition-driven step-change, rapid deleveraging, and, finally, the modest but symbolically weighted first return of cash to shareholders. Whether the arc continued upward depended on execution tests still outstanding — but the quarterly cadence, at least, had made its case.

chapters.title: The Krebs Era: Fifteen Years of CEO Continuity, Capital Discipline, and Deal-Making
chapters.body:
## A Financier Who Learned to Mine

Mitchell J. Krebs arrived at Coeur d'Alene Mines in 1995 as something of an anomaly. Most silver miners of that era were built from the geology up — geologists, engineers, or operating veterans who had spent years underground before reaching the executive suite. Krebs came from New York investment banking, bearing a Bachelor of Science in Economics from the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and, later, an MBA from Harvard Business School. His orientation was toward capital structures and deal books, not ore grades and mill recoveries. Over the following sixteen years, working through progressively senior roles in the corporate development department before reaching Senior Vice President, he developed a miner's discipline to accompany the financier's instincts. When the board elevated him to President and Chief Executive Officer in 2011, he became — and would remain, fifteen years later — one of the longest-tenured chief executives among US-listed precious-metals producers, a peer group not known for stability at the top.

That biographical arc matters because it shaped every significant decision of his tenure. Unlike a geologist-turned-CEO, Krebs has consistently framed strategic choices in the language of capital allocation: return on invested capital, net asset value per share, leverage ratios, and free cash flow yield. The mining industry rewards operators; it punishes over-leveraged acquirers. Krebs has spent fifteen years learning to be both.

## The Crucible: 2015–2016 and the Education in Humility

The most consequential period of the Krebs era did not involve a major acquisition or a triumphant expansion. It was, instead, a near-death experience. Silver prices, which had peaked at roughly $49 per ounce in April 2011 — the month Krebs took the CEO role — entered a sustained collapse that carried the metal below $14 per ounce by late 2015. Coeur, which had been aggressively building its international portfolio, found itself carrying debt it could not comfortably service against assets generating cash flows that had shrunk dramatically. The company was not alone in its distress — the entire silver-mining sector was under pressure — but Coeur's balance sheet had less cushion than its size implied.

The response revealed the character of the executive team. Krebs moved systematically through the asset portfolio, identifying non-core operations that consumed capital without justifying their position in the portfolio. The company divested or wound down several international positions, reduced operating costs across the remaining mines through workforce rationalisation and contractor renegotiation, and accessed the equity markets despite the severe dilution cost. None of these decisions were popular. All of them were necessary.

What the 2015–2016 crisis instilled was a lasting conservatism about debt and a near-obsessive focus on cost-per-ounce discipline at the operating level. Krebs has referenced that period repeatedly in the years since as the formative constraint on the company's capital allocation philosophy. Before Las Chispas, before the Rochester expansion consumed $730 million, before New Gold, the lesson from the silver-price collapse shaped every subsequent decision about how much leverage to carry and how quickly to reduce it when circumstances permitted.

## The CFO Partnership: Thomas Whelan and the Architecture of Deleveraging

Thomas S. Whelan joined Coeur as Chief Financial Officer in 2019, arriving from Arizona Mining — a silver-zinc developer in which South32 had seen sufficient merit to pay $1.3 billion for a full acquisition in 2018. The Arizona Mining experience gave Whelan a particular perspective: he had seen a single-project developer taken out at a substantial premium, but he had also worked through the final stages of advancing a capital-intensive project through feasibility and construction. The move from a lean developer to a multi-asset producer operating in five jurisdictions represented a significant expansion of scope.

Whelan's most visible contribution to the Krebs era came in 2025, when Coeur deployed its Rochester-generated free cash flow and Las Chispas earnings with unusual speed against its debt stack. [Total debt declined from $590 million at year-end 2024 to $341 million at year-end 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000215466/000114036125011870/ny20041389x1_def14a.htm) — a 42 percent reduction in a single fiscal year that no prior management team had achieved. The sequencing reflected deliberate CFO-level design: rather than reinvesting the free cash flow surge into exploration or bolt-on acquisitions, Whelan structured the capital allocation to demonstrate to debt and equity markets alike that the Rochester capital cycle was genuinely over and that the company's financial architecture had moved permanently away from the leveraged model that nearly proved fatal in 2016. That signal — delivered in a year when the company was also integrating Las Chispas, managing the post-close of a $1.7 billion acquisition, and preparing the New Gold transaction — carried substantial credibility.

## The Board: Refreshment, Expertise, and Independence

The Coeur board that oversaw the two major acquisitions of 2024–2026 was meaningfully different from the board that had navigated the 2015–2016 distress. Independent Chairman Robert E. Mellor leads a nine-member group that, as of the 2025 proxy, included four directors added in the preceding three years — a refreshment cadence that reflects both the company's expanded scale and the demands of more complex governance oversight.

The most operationally significant of the recent additions was Rob Krcmarov, appointed to the board in December 2023. Krcmarov served as Chief Exploration Officer at Barrick Gold, one of the world's largest gold miners, before his appointment — a résumé that carries particular relevance given Coeur's stated ambition to grow reserves organically at its highest-grade assets. His arrival on the board preceded by less than a year the announcement of the SilverCrest acquisition, and his exploration expertise has likely informed the company's commitment to expanding the 2026 exploration budget to $120–136 million. Palmarejo, Kensington, and the Silvertip project in British Columbia are the primary targets of that capital; Krcmarov's presence at the board level provides a form of technical validation for exploration investment decisions that most financially-oriented boards would scrutinise sceptically.

The governance structure is entirely public-market facing, with no private equity sponsor and no controlling shareholder bloc. That independence has given Krebs and his team unusual strategic flexibility — both the SilverCrest and New Gold transactions were executed without activist pressure or sponsor-driven timelines — but it also means that market sentiment, quarterly earnings delivery, and institutional shareholder opinion serve as the primary accountability mechanism.

## Compensation: Performance Aligned, Governance Endorsed

The 2025 compensation cycle provided an unusually clear signal of board-management alignment. The Annual Incentive Plan paid out at [133 percent of target](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000215466/000114036125011870/ny20041389x1_def14a.htm), reflecting the record operating performance, successful Las Chispas integration, and safety milestones achieved across the seven-mine portfolio. The Long-Term Incentive Plan paid out at 166 percent of target, calibrated to multi-year total shareholder return, NAV growth, and strategic milestone completion — metrics that rewarded the completion of the Rochester expansion and the structural improvement in free cash flow generation. Shareholders endorsed both outcomes: the say-on-pay resolution received greater than 97 percent support at the 2025 annual meeting, an endorsement that is difficult to achieve when compensation structures are perceived as misaligned with shareholder interests.

## The New Gold Question: Integration Leadership and Succession Depth

The March 2026 close of the New Gold transaction raised a governance question that is material to any assessment of Coeur's management depth: what role, if any, would Renaud Adams, New Gold's former President and Chief Executive Officer, play in the combined organisation? Adams is among the more respected operating executives in the Canadian gold sector; his tenure at New Gold oversaw the development of Rainy River and the advance of the K-Zone at New Afton. Available 8-K disclosures and proxy materials through the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026 do not confirm Adams's appointment to either the Coeur board or the executive team. The absence of a disclosed transition role for a CEO of Adams's profile is not unusual — acquirer management teams rarely retain target CEOs in operating roles — but it does concentrate integration execution authority firmly in Krebs's existing team.

That concentration is the most significant governance risk in the Krebs era. A fifteen-year CEO tenure is a strength in a sector where institutional knowledge compounds; it is also a key-person dependency that becomes acute when the organisation's complexity doubles in eighteen months. Coeur's proxy identifies a leadership bench that includes Whelan at CFO and operational vice presidents across the mine portfolio, but the strategic direction of the combined seven-mine company — spanning five jurisdictions, two streaming obligations, a copper concentrate business, and a $3 billion EBITDA target — runs through Krebs with unusual concentration.

## The Deal Fingerprint: Capital Allocation as Competitive Advantage

What the SilverCrest and New Gold acquisitions share — beyond their all-stock structures — is a common logic of timing. Both deals were executed not when target valuations were depressed by sector pessimism, nor when competitive bidding drove prices to premium territory. Instead, both were structured to capture operational inflection points at the target company: Las Chispas had demonstrated its cost profile at scale but had not yet been re-rated by the market as a tier-one asset; New Gold's Rainy River and New Afton operations had stabilised after years of capital-intensity and mine-plan revision, providing a clearer floor on downside risk. In both cases Coeur offered exchange ratios that implied no meaningful premium to net asset value — a structuring discipline that an investment banker turned mining CEO would recognise as the difference between a value-creating deal and a value-transferring one.

The result is a transaction history that looks, in retrospect, less like the serial acquirer's impulse to grow for its own sake and more like the application of a consistent capital-allocation framework across a decade and a half of changing commodity cycles. Whether that framework can hold at the scale Coeur has now reached — with a market capitalisation near $18.8 billion and seven mines demanding simultaneous management attention — is the central question the Krebs era has not yet answered.

chapters.title: End Markets, Streaming Obligations, and the Silver Industrial Demand Tailwind
chapters.body:
## A Price-Taker in a Spot Market

Coeur Mining's commercial model is deliberately simple. The company digs silver and gold from the ground, pours it into doré bars — unrefined alloys of roughly 60–95 percent precious metal — and ships those bars to third-party refineries where they are processed to London Good Delivery standard. The refined metal then enters the global spot market through bullion banks and commodity traders, ultimately reaching industrial consumers, jewellers, central banks, or exchange-traded fund vaults. At no point in that chain does Coeur control the price it receives. It is, in the industry's own terminology, a pure price-taker: revenue moves in lock-step with the London Bullion Market Association silver fix and the COMEX gold settlement, adjusted for transport and refining costs that run a few dollars per ounce.

That architecture is a conscious strategic choice. Coeur carries no material forward-sale hedging book. Management articulated this posture repeatedly through the 2013–2016 silver price collapse and has not retreated from it since. The logic is that investors who buy CDE shares are seeking unhedged leverage to silver and gold prices; inserting a derivatives overlay that caps upside would replicate the economics of a royalty or streaming company without the royalty company's lower operating cost structure. In 2025, with silver averaging approximately $31–32 per ounce during the first half of the year before accelerating sharply into 2026 guidance territory of $77.50 per ounce, the absence of hedges delivered extraordinary upside to Coeur's revenue line: full-year 2025 revenue reached $2.1 billion, nearly double the $1.1 billion reported in 2024, and first-quarter 2026 revenue of $856 million — with New Gold contributing only eleven days — annualises to more than $3.4 billion on a full-portfolio basis.

## The Franco-Nevada Overhang at Palmarejo

The one exception to Coeur's unhedged posture is not of its own making. When Coeur acquired the Palmarejo silver-gold mine in Chihuahua, Mexico in 2007, it simultaneously entered a gold streaming agreement with Franco-Nevada Corporation that remains in force today and constitutes the single largest structural drag on the company's revenue realisation. Under the stream, Franco-Nevada is entitled to purchase approximately 40–50 percent of Palmarejo's annual gold production at a fixed price of $800 per ounce — a price set when gold was trading near $700 and that has become progressively more punitive as the gold price has appreciated over nearly two decades.

The arithmetic is stark. Palmarejo produced 100,768 gold ounces in fiscal year 2025. Applying the stream's entitlement at the midpoint of the disclosed range implies roughly 44,000–50,000 ounces delivered to Franco-Nevada at $800 per ounce, generating approximately $35–40 million in stream revenue. Had those same ounces been sold at Coeur's 2026 guidance gold price of $4,550 per ounce, the revenue would have been approximately $200–228 million — a differential of roughly $160–190 million per year that never reaches Coeur's income statement. Over a full market cycle, the Franco-Nevada stream functions as a permanent royalty that strips a material fraction of Palmarejo's gold economics and transfers it to the counterparty. The company acknowledges this in its annual filings, disclosing the stream among the principal risk factors affecting realised gold prices.

The streaming obligation does not affect silver production at Palmarejo, which is sold into the spot market at full realised prices, nor does it touch Las Chispas, Rochester, Kensington, Wharf, Rainy River, or New Afton. Its impact is therefore mine-specific rather than portfolio-wide. But because Palmarejo is one of Coeur's more productive gold contributors — 100,768 ounces in 2025 placing it second among the legacy five mines behind Kensington's roughly 110,000-ounce cadence — the revenue foregone is meaningful at the consolidated level and represents the clearest structural inefficiency in Coeur's end-market architecture.

## Copper Enters the Revenue Mix

The March 2026 acquisition of New Gold introduced a fundamentally new commodity into Coeur's sales portfolio: copper. The New Afton block-cave mine near Kamloops, British Columbia produces a gold-copper concentrate — a mixed sulphide product rather than doré — that is sold to smelters rather than refineries. The distinction matters commercially. Concentrate sales involve treatment charges (TCs) paid to the smelter per dry metric tonne of concentrate processed and refining charges (RCs) paid per pound of copper recovered, both of which reduce net revenue relative to the contained metal value. Payable metal ratios — the percentage of gold and copper in the concentrate that the smelter credits to the seller — are negotiated annually with reference to Pacific Basin benchmark terms, which in recent years have reflected a tightening smelter market as Chinese capacity has grown more selective about feedstock quality.

Coeur's 2026 production guidance incorporates 50–65 million pounds of copper from New Afton. At a copper price near $4.50–5.00 per pound, that represents gross contained copper revenue of approximately $225–325 million before TC/RC deductions, treatment losses, and transport. Copper payability at a well-run block-cave like New Afton typically runs 96–97 percent of London Metal Exchange settlement, broadly comparable to gold payability at a doré refinery but slightly lower on a percentage basis. The net contribution from copper is expected to be material enough that Coeur now discloses copper guidance in its investor materials and analysts routinely model it as a distinct revenue line — a departure from the company's prior identity as a pure precious-metals producer.

## The Silver Industrial Demand Tailwind

The macroeconomic backdrop for Coeur's silver business has shifted meaningfully during the company's transformation period. Silver is simultaneously an investment metal — historically trading in loose correlation with gold — and an industrial input that cannot easily be substituted in its most demanding applications. Photovoltaic panels require silver paste as an electrical conductor; a single utility-scale solar installation consumes thousands of ounces. Automotive electronics, including the battery management systems and power electronics in electric vehicles, consume silver in quantities that rise with vehicle electrification content. Global photovoltaic installation rates have accelerated sharply in the 2020s, and the structural growth in EV penetration adds a demand vector that did not exist at meaningful scale when Coeur's current balance sheet crisis was playing out a decade ago.

The consequence has been a silver market in which industrial demand growth has consistently outpaced new mine supply additions — a dynamic that contributed to the silver price's appreciation from roughly $23–26 per ounce during Coeur's 2021–2023 capital-intensive years to the $77.50 per ounce embedded in 2026 guidance. As a primary silver producer — meaning a company that mines silver as a principal product rather than a by-product of copper or zinc — Coeur captures the full benefit of that price appreciation across its production base. Las Chispas alone is expected to produce approximately 10–11 million silver equivalent ounces annually; Rochester adds a further 7–9 million ounces of silver production per year at full POA 11 ramp. Each one-dollar increase in the silver price translates directly into roughly $17–20 million of incremental annual revenue across those two assets at current production rates.

## Geographic Concentration and Counterparty Structure

Coeur's seven-mine footprint spans four countries and five fiscal jurisdictions, and its refinery and smelter relationships reflect that geographic spread. Las Chispas and Palmarejo operate under Mexican fiscal regimes; doré produced at both mines is processed by refineries operating within or contractually accessible from Mexico, with the company subject to Mexican value-added tax recovery cycles that have periodically created working capital timing friction. Nevada (Rochester) and South Dakota (Wharf) sell to US-based refineries under standard domestic commercial terms. Kensington, in Alaska, ships doré to mainland US refiners under logistics arrangements that include maritime transport from the remote coastal site. The two Canadian operations — Rainy River and New Afton — have their own refinery and smelter relationships reflecting Canadian and Pacific Basin commercial norms.

Coeur has historically disclosed in its SEC filings that no single commercial refinery customer accounts for more than a defined concentration threshold of consolidated revenue, consistent with the commoditised, spot-market nature of doré sales. Franco-Nevada is the one disclosed contractual counterparty of significance, given the structured streaming arrangement rather than an arm's-length spot transaction. Outside that stream, the company does not hold long-term off-take agreements on any of its seven mines — a structure that maximises participation in rising price environments but exposes revenue to the full amplitude of commodity price cycles. In 2023, when silver traded near $23, that exposure compressed margins to near-breakeven at Rochester and rendered the balance sheet vulnerable; in 2026, at $77.50, the identical structure generates cash flows that management projects will fund nearly $2 billion of free cash flow annually.

The absence of off-take agreements is, in this sense, a deliberate asymmetry: Coeur accepted the downside volatility of the spot market in exchange for unrestricted participation in the upside — a bet that has paid off dramatically in the 2025–2026 precious metals cycle, and one that the company has no stated intention of altering for any mine outside the legacy Franco-Nevada obligation it inherited and cannot unilaterally terminate.

chapters.title: Peers, Pricing, and the Mid-Tier Positioning Question After Two Transformative Acquisitions
chapters.body:
## From Balance-Sheet-Stressed Mid-Tier to Large-Cap Operator

In 2023, Coeur Mining occupied an uncomfortable position in the precious-metals equity universe. Its peer group was Hecla Mining, First Majestic Silver, and Endeavour Silver — companies defined less by operational excellence than by shared exposure to silver price volatility and capital structures that left little margin for error. Coeur's CDE shares traded in the $4–5 range through much of that year, weighed down by the $730 million Rochester POA 11 capital burn and a net leverage ratio that had risen toward 1.7x as the project consumed cash. The Rochester expansion, the most expensive undertaking in the company's 97-year history, had yet to deliver the throughput economics that justified the outlay, and the balance sheet bore the evidence: debt-financed capital spending at a moment when the silver price offered little buffer.

By May 2026, the competitive coordinate had shifted to a different map entirely. With the close of the New Gold transaction on March 20, 2026, Coeur's market capitalisation reached approximately $18.8 billion — placing it above Hecla, First Majestic, Pan American Silver, and Endeavour Silver, and into the same zip code as Kinross Gold and Iamgold. The company's 2026 production guidance of 680,000–815,000 gold ounces, 18.7–21.9 million silver ounces, and 50–65 million copper pounds from New Afton is no longer a silver-weighted mid-tier profile; it is a diversified North American precious-metals and base-metals conglomerate of a kind that did not exist under the Coeur banner three years earlier.

## The Peer Map Redrawn

The shift in peer group is best understood through production scale and market capitalisation together.

| Company | Approx. Market Cap (May 2026) | Gold Production (est. 2026) | Silver Production (est. 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coeur Mining (CDE) | ~$18.8B | 680,000–815,000 oz | 18.7–21.9 M oz |
| Kinross Gold (KGC) | ~$22–25B | ~2.0–2.1 M oz | — (minor) |
| Iamgold (IAG) | ~$5–7B | ~500,000–600,000 oz | — |
| Pan American Silver (PAAS) | ~$8–10B | ~500,000–600,000 oz Au-eq | ~20–22 M oz Ag |
| Hecla Mining (HL) | ~$4–5B | ~60,000 oz | ~15–16 M oz Ag |
| First Majestic Silver (AG) | ~$3–4B | ~100,000 oz | ~20–22 M oz Ag |

Coeur is no longer competing for Hecla's investors. The company's gold production alone, anchored by Rainy River and New Afton from the New Gold acquisition and Kensington and Wharf from the legacy portfolio, places it closer to the mid-range of the senior North American gold producer category. Pan American Silver is the most directly comparable silver-weighted large-cap operator, and Coeur's production envelope now exceeds Pan American's on gold while broadly matching it on silver — a symmetry that makes the two companies natural valuation reference points for generalist precious-metals allocators.

The repositioning was not merely quantitative. Prior to the SilverCrest transaction, Coeur lacked a flagship low-cost silver asset capable of anchoring its investment thesis for dedicated silver investors. Las Chispas, with its sub-$11 per-ounce adjusted cash costs in operating quarters and its narrow-vein high-grade underground profile, filled that role immediately upon closing in February 2025.

## The Streaming Discount: A Structural Ceiling

Coeur's approximately 6x EV/EBITDA multiple on 2026 guided EBITDA reflects a gap that no amount of operational execution is likely to close entirely. Franco-Nevada, Royal Gold, and Wheaton Precious Metals trade at 10–15x EBITDA — a premium that is not a market inefficiency but a structural reward for business model characteristics that Coeur, as an operator, cannot replicate.

Streaming and royalty companies carry none of the operating cost exposure that defines — and periodically torments — producing miners. They bear no capital expenditure obligations beyond the upfront stream purchase, no labour risk, no environmental liability, and no geotechnical exposure. When Rochester's Stage 6 leach pad required additional capital, Coeur bore it entirely; under a streaming structure, the operator would. The royalty model monetises the same metal price upside through a structurally superior risk-adjusted cash flow profile, and the equity market has consistently capitalised that difference at premium multiples for the better part of two decades.

There is an additional irony in Coeur's own streaming exposure. The Franco-Nevada gold stream at Palmarejo — under which approximately 40–50 percent of Palmarejo's annual gold production is delivered at a fixed price of $800 per ounce — is precisely the mechanism that allowed Coeur to finance Palmarejo's development in 2009 while transferring upside to Franco-Nevada at a fraction of the then-spot gold price. At $4,550/oz gold, that obligation now represents a material drag on realised gold revenue at Palmarejo; it is, in effect, Coeur subsidising Franco-Nevada's premium multiple from the other side of the trade.

## Cost Positions Across the Portfolio

Coeur's post-acquisition cost profile is bifurcated in ways that matter for the valuation conversation.

| Asset | Primary Metal | Adjusted CAS (2025) | Peer Context |
|---|---|---|---|
| Las Chispas | Silver | ~$10.75/oz Ag (Q3 2025) | Best-in-class among primary silver producers |
| Palmarejo | Gold | ~$871/oz Au | Competitive mid-tier; streaming drag reduces net realisation |
| Wharf | Gold | ~$1,151/oz Au | Competitive for open-pit South Dakota geology |
| Rochester | Silver | ~$18.39/oz Ag (FY 2025) | Above primary silver producer median; ramp-in progress |
| Kensington | Gold | ~$1,685/oz Au | Upper quartile of gold production costs |

Las Chispas at approximately $10.75 per silver ounce in Q3 2025 is the portfolio's crown jewel and the strategic justification for the $1.7 billion SilverCrest acquisition. No primary silver producer in North America consistently operates below that cost level; the closest comparisons are select underground operations in Mexico and Peru where mineralisation grades approach or exceed Las Chispas's 500–700 gram-per-tonne AgEq profile. The challenge, as the broader dossier addresses, is whether Coeur can preserve those costs as integration overhead accumulates.

Kensington's cost structure requires specific context. The mine operates underground in a remote location approximately 45 miles north of Juneau, Alaska — accessible by sea or air only, with no road connection to the continental highway grid. All supplies, personnel, and equipment move by barge or aircraft. The combination of underground mining at moderate grades, Alaskan labour market wage premiums, and logistics-driven operating cost inflation structurally positions Kensington above the median gold producer cost curve. At $1,685 per ounce in 2025, Kensington remains profitable at $4,550/oz gold but would become marginal — and cash-flow-negative after sustaining capital — in a return to $2,000/oz gold conditions. That sensitivity is not hypothetical: Kensington operated at a loss during portions of the 2015–2016 gold price trough.

## Private Developers and the Acquisition Pipeline

SilverCrest's Las Chispas was the most prominent example of a TSX-listed silver-gold developer that Coeur absorbed — a company that had built one of the decade's most impressive greenfield-to-production track records before agreeing to a takeout at approximately $1.7 billion. The acquisition removed a genuine competitive threat: Las Chispas, under SilverCrest's continued ownership, would have grown into a sub-10-dollar-cost silver producer with balance sheet capacity to pursue its own secondary acquisitions.

The remaining private developer landscape includes names that represent either future acquisition targets or structural cost benchmarks that pressure Coeur's portfolio optics. MAG Silver's Juanicipio joint venture with Fresnillo in Zacatecas, Mexico, operates at ultra-high grades in the same Mexican silver belt where Las Chispas sits; it is not available for acquisition given Fresnillo's 56 percent operator interest, but it demonstrates that best-in-class Mexican silver costs are achievable and replicable. Silver One Resources and Silverton Metals are earlier-stage developers whose current scale does not move Coeur's needle meaningfully, though their existence attests to the continued generation of high-grade silver-gold exploration targets in the Americas.

The more consequential competitive dynamic is geological scarcity. Tier-1 silver-gold underground assets with proven grades above 400 grams per tonne AgEq and established infrastructure are rare, and the universe of available targets capable of transforming Coeur's portfolio at the Las Chispas level is effectively exhausted for the medium term.

## Situating Coeur in the Consolidation Wave

Coeur's two acquisitions were not idiosyncratic; they were executed inside a broader 2024–2026 precious-metals M&A cycle driven by elevated spot prices, compressed valuations of junior and mid-tier operators relative to metal price appreciation, and senior producers seeking production growth without greenfield capital risk. Gold Fields' acquisition of Osisko Mining's Windfall project, Agnico Eagle's portfolio bolt-ons in the Abitibi camp, and Pan American Silver's asset rationalisation moves all reflect the same structural logic: scale advantages, overhead absorption, and the premium that capital markets assign to operators with diversified, politically stable production bases.

Within that wave, Coeur's serial acquisition model — two all-stock transactions within eighteen months, funded entirely by share issuance rather than debt — distinguishes it from peers who pursued cash-and-debt combinations that left balance sheets strained. The all-stock approach preserved financial flexibility at the cost of substantial dilution; shares outstanding expanded 2.6 times between year-end 2024 and the May 2026 snapshot. Whether that dilution is ultimately justified depends on whether the per-share cash flow growth from two combined portfolios outpaces the per-share count expansion — the central arithmetic of the dossier's bull case.

chapters.title: Timeline of Triggers: From Rochester Commercial Production to the New Gold Close and Beyond
chapters.body:
## The Foundational Trigger: Commercial Production at Rochester

On March 31, 2024, Coeur Mining declared commercial production at its enlarged Rochester heap-leach operation in Pershing County, Nevada — a sentence that carried the weight of five years of financial strain. The $730 million Plan of Operations Amendment 11 expansion had required successive equity issuances, debt drawings, and revised project timelines that tested investor patience and, more acutely, the company's credit profile. CDE shares, which had traded near $4–5 during the capital peak of 2023, absorbed the declaration calmly: the announcement confirmed that the capital spending was complete, not that the throughput economics had been proven.
