That proof would take another year to accumulate.

The commercial-production declaration nonetheless reset the company's investment narrative. Rochester was no longer a capital sink; it was a production asset in ramp-up. The implied trajectory — 32 million tonnes per year of ore processed through one of North America's largest Merrill-Crowe facilities — would, if achieved, transform what had been Coeur's most expensive open-pit mine into one of its highest-volume silver contributors. By full-year 2025 Rochester delivered 6.1 million silver ounces and 60,178 gold ounces at an adjusted cost of $18.39 per silver ounce, representing real progress, if not yet the cost compression required to fully vindicate the capital expenditure.

## SilverCrest: The Acquisition That Changed the Thesis

Six months after Rochester's commercial-production milestone, Coeur pivoted from defence to offence. On October 4, 2024, the company announced an all-stock agreement to acquire SilverCrest Metals Inc. in a transaction implying approximately $1.7 billion of equity value — at 1.6022 Coeur shares per SilverCrest share. The deal was not incremental; it was re-rating. Las Chispas, SilverCrest's underground silver-gold mine in Sonora, Mexico, was widely regarded as the highest-grade primary silver mine in commercial production anywhere in the world, with all-in sustaining costs that had consistently ranked among the sector's lowest.

The announcement triggered an immediate re-rating of CDE. Shares moved toward the $9–10 range by the time the transaction closed in February 2025 following Mexican antitrust clearance from COFECE. In its first partial quarter of Coeur ownership — approximately six weeks — Las Chispas contributed 714,239 silver ounces and 7,175 gold ounces at an adjusted cost of $8.38 per ounce of silver, validating the asset's quality thesis. The combined company entered 2025 with a fundamentally different earnings profile: where 2024 revenue had reached approximately $1.1 billion, the 2025 full year would ultimately record $2.1 billion — a near-doubling driven equally by Las Chispas, Rochester's ramp, and rising commodity prices.

## Record EBITDA and the New Gold Gambit

By the third quarter of 2025, the financial story had become empirically impressive. Coeur reported record quarterly EBITDA, a milestone that management used to frame the logic of what came next. On November 3, 2025, the company announced a definitive arrangement agreement to acquire New Gold Inc. in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $7 billion — an exchange ratio of 0.4959 Coeur shares per New Gold share. The transaction would add the Rainy River gold-silver mine in northwestern Ontario and the New Afton gold-copper block-cave operation near Kamloops, British Columbia, adding an estimated 430,000–480,000 gold ounces and 50–65 million copper pounds to the 2026 production envelope.

The November announcement prompted both enthusiasm and scepticism. The combination was expected to generate approximately $3 billion of annual EBITDA and $2 billion of free cash flow in 2026 — figures that, at the time of announcement, represented a step-change in Coeur's scale. But Rainy River carried a track record of capital overruns and near-term mine-plan revision risk, and the share count implications were stark: combined with the SilverCrest dilution, shares outstanding would expand from approximately 399 million at year-end 2024 to approximately 1.03 billion by the time the New Gold transaction closed.

## February 2026: The Year That Was

When Coeur reported full-year 2025 results in February 2026, the numbers crystallised the scale of the transformation. Net income reached $586 million against $59 million in 2024. Adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 billion compared with $339 million the prior year. Free cash flow of $666 million reversed from negative $9 million — a $675 million swing that funded $249 million of debt repayment and left the company with $554 million of cash at year-end. Total debt fell 42 percent to $341 million, and the net leverage ratio had already moved to a net-cash position. The mineral reserves update accompanying the results extended Wharf's mine life to approximately twelve years following a reserve restatement that doubled the South Dakota mine's declared reserve base.

The New Gold transaction received all required regulatory approvals and closed on March 20, 2026. Coeur's Q1 2026 report, which included only eleven days of New Gold contribution, nonetheless recorded revenue of $856 million and adjusted EBITDA of $475 million — a quarterly run rate implying approximately $1.9 billion of full-year EBITDA on the legacy five-mine portfolio alone, before the full-year Canadian contribution.

## The Inaugural Dividend: A Signal, Not Just a Payment

In May 2026, Coeur declared a semi-annual cash dividend of $0.02 per share — its first dividend in the modern era. At $0.04 annualised on a $18.34 share price, the yield was negligible. The financial significance lay elsewhere: the declaration marked the company's formal exit from the balance-sheet-repair phase and its entry into a capital-return framework. It was a signal to institutional holders that management viewed the earnings base as durable, not cyclical. CDE shares had already reached approximately $18.34 by late May 2026 — roughly 3.5x their 2023 lows and 2x their post-SilverCrest trading range.

## Commodity Prices: The Variable That Rewrites Every Model

Coeur's 2026 guidance rests on gold at $4,550 per ounce and silver at $77.50 per ounce. Contextualised against history, both assumptions are structurally extraordinary. The 20-year realised average for gold through 2024 approximates $1,400–$1,500 per ounce; at $4,550, gold is trading at roughly three times its long-run average. Silver's 20-year average approximates $18–$22 per ounce; at $77.50, the ratio approaches four times the historical baseline.

The sensitivity arithmetic is unforgiving in both directions. A $500/oz decline in gold from guidance levels — a move of roughly 11 percent — would reduce Coeur's 2026 free cash flow by an estimated $200–250 million on a combined-mine basis, given approximately 430,000–480,000 gold ounces from the Canadian assets alone. A silver price correction of $15/oz from the $77.50 assumption would erode margins at Rochester and Las Chispas proportionally. Conversely, further appreciation compounds rapidly: the combination of high operating leverage at Rochester, ultra-low costs at Las Chispas, and the scale of New Afton's gold-copper production creates meaningful torque to commodity prices above guidance.

| Commodity | 20-Year Avg (est.) | 2026 Guidance Assumption | Premium to 20-Year Avg |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gold (USD/oz) | ~$1,450 | $4,550 | ~214% |
| Silver (USD/oz) | ~$20 | $77.50 | ~288% |

## The Cash Tax Headwind and Forward Catalysts

One earnings variable conspicuously absent from consensus models is the 2026 cash tax obligation. Management guided $400–500 million of cash taxes for the year — a figure that reflects the company's heavily profitable operating environment but will represent the single largest cash outflow claim on free cash flow after sustaining capital. The obligation spans multiple jurisdictions: Mexico (Las Chispas, Palmarejo), the United States (Rochester, Kensington, Wharf), and Canada (Rainy River, New Afton), each with distinct effective rates and deferred tax asset positions from prior-year losses. The Mexican operations, which carry among the highest margins in the portfolio, will likely bear the greatest proportional burden. To the extent consensus models have modelled statutory rates rather than cash taxes net of deferred asset utilisation, the per-share earnings headwind may surprise.

From the May 2026 vantage point, four catalysts stand to define the balance of the year and 2027. At New Afton, K-Zone underground development progress represents the most consequential forward variable: a successful extension of the block-cave footprint would materially extend mine life and justify the acquisition premium embedded in the $7 billion transaction. At Rainy River, a mine-plan update expected in 2026 will clarify the asset's capital requirements and production trajectory — the outcome most likely to either validate or challenge the deal rationale. At Palmarejo, exploration results from areas outside the Franco-Nevada stream-affected zone could identify mineralisation that Coeur captures at full market prices, not at the structurally discounted $800-per-ounce stream rate. And at Rochester, whether throughput achieves the 32 million tonne per year design capacity remains an open question — 2025 demonstrated progress toward that target, but final confirmation would close the book on a five-year capital cycle. The Silvertip polymetallic project in northern British Columbia has a pre-feasibility study on an unconfirmed timeline; any positive study publication would reintroduce a development-capex narrative to a market that has rewarded capital discipline.

chapters.title: Heap Leach Optimisation, Exploration Drilling, and the Geology-Driven IP Framework
chapters.body:
## The Absence of a Patent Portfolio Is Not a Weakness

Coeur Mining holds no meaningful patent portfolio, carries no software-licensing revenue line, and operates no trademark of commercial significance beyond the corporate name. A securities attorney reviewing the company's intellectual property disclosures in its annual filings would find them perfunctory — a handful of boilerplate paragraphs acknowledging that the company relies on trade secrets and operational know-how. This is not a deficiency. It is a structural feature of the precious-metals mining industry, where competitive differentiation does not arise from registered intellectual property but from the accumulated, non-replicable understanding of what lies underground and how to extract it profitably.

The relevant IP equivalents in mining are geological models, grade-control methodology, processing-circuit optimisation, geomechanical engineering, and — critically — the permitted operating licences and environmental approvals that represent years of regulatory work and serve as genuine moats against new entrants. By these measures, Coeur's knowledge base across its seven-mine portfolio as of May 2026 represents a formidable and largely unquantified asset.

## Rochester: The Merrill-Crowe Process as Accumulated Operating Expertise

The most tangible example of operational knowledge functioning as proprietary capability is the Rochester heap-leach complex in Pershing County, Nevada. The $730 million Plan of Operations Amendment 11 expansion did not merely install physical infrastructure — leach pad stages, crushing circuits, conveyors, and one of the largest Merrill-Crowe processing facilities in North America. It also generated, through years of iterative commissioning and process calibration, an engineering-level understanding of how Rochester's specific ore body responds to cyanide heap-leach chemistry at industrial scale.

The Merrill-Crowe process — which strips dissolved precious metals from pregnant leach solution through zinc precipitation — is a mature industrial technology, but its optimisation at any given ore body is site-specific and operationally sensitive. Leach-pad chemistry management at Rochester requires continuous adjustment of solution application rates, reagent dosing, and pad drainage protocols as the ore's mineralogical characteristics vary across different sectors of the Stage 6 and prior pad stages. Crushing-circuit throughput maximisation demands an intimate understanding of the ore's hardness distribution and how it interacts with the three-stage crushing configuration installed under POA 11.

By the fourth quarter of 2025, those calibration efforts were beginning to manifest in measurable results. Mitchell Krebs pointed to "record crushing and placement rates" during the Q4 2025 earnings call, describing Rochester's operational cadence as approaching the design throughput envelope the team had targeted since POA 11's commercial production declaration in March 2024. Full-year 2025 production of 6.1 million silver ounces and 60,178 gold ounces reflected a mine still in ramp mode, but the throughput trajectory it established — and the process knowledge embedded in Rochester's operating teams — represents operational IP that a would-be competitor could not acquire simply by building similar equipment.

## Palmarejo: The East Corridor Geological Model

If Rochester's IP is process-driven, Palmarejo's is geological. The Palmarejo mine in Chihuahua, Mexico, has operated since 2009, and Coeur's exploration teams have spent the intervening years assembling a detailed three-dimensional understanding of the epithermal vein systems that host silver and gold mineralisation across the broader Palmarejo district.

The East Palmarejo exploration corridor demonstrated the value of that accumulated knowledge most concretely in 2025, when a systematic drilling programme targeting extensions of known vein structures yielded maiden inferred resource additions at the San Miguel, La Union, and Independencia Sur prospects. The combined effect of those additions drove an 86 percent increase in Palmarejo's inferred resource base — a step-change in the mine's geological inventory that could not have been designed without the district-scale geological framework Coeur's team had constructed over fifteen years of continuous study.

That framework — the structural mapping, alteration geochemistry, fluid inclusion data, and predictive vectoring models that guide drill-hole targeting — constitutes a form of intellectual capital. A new entrant to the Palmarejo district would face not just the cost of exploration drilling but the multi-year knowledge deficit that makes drill-hole targeting efficient rather than speculative.

## Las Chispas: Narrow-Vein Grade Control as Integration Risk

The Las Chispas mine in Sonora, Mexico, operates on a fundamentally different geological template. The Babicanora vein system — the principal ore structure developed by SilverCrest Metals before the February 2025 acquisition — is characterised by high-grade, narrow veins whose economic viability depends entirely on the precision of underground drilling and grade-control methodology. SilverCrest developed this methodology over four years of owner-operated underground development, building a mine crew whose institutional knowledge of the Babicanora system's structural geometry and grade distribution was embedded in the operating team itself.

Maintaining that precision under Coeur's larger operating structure is one of the company's most consequential integration risks. The geological model for Las Chispas is not portable in a spreadsheet. It lives in the judgements of underground geologists who know where the veins widen, where they pinch, and where dilution risk is highest. Organisational turnover, the imposition of standardised Coeur operating procedures, and the inevitable friction of absorbing a single-asset company into a seven-mine bureaucracy all represent threats to the grade-control discipline that made Las Chispas the lowest-cost silver mine in the Western Hemisphere.

## New Afton: Geomechanical Engineering as Value Creation

The K-Zone resource at New Afton near Kamloops, British Columbia — defined in technical reports filed in March 2026 — represents an initial resource of 47.6 million tonnes grading approximately 715,000 ounces of gold, 2.9 million ounces of silver, and 606 million pounds of copper. The block-cave mining method proposed for the K-Zone's development is among the most technically demanding in underground mining. It depends on rigorous geomechanical modelling to predict how the host rock mass will fracture, cave, and draw through extraction drifts — a failure to model cave propagation accurately can result in either premature hang-ups that halt production or uncontrolled subsidence that endangers surface infrastructure.

New Gold's engineering team developed this geomechanical understanding through years of work at the existing B3/C-Zone block cave; Coeur's value from the K-Zone extension depends materially on retaining and integrating that team's knowledge.

## The 2026 Exploration Programme

Against this backdrop, Coeur's guided exploration budget of $120–136 million for 2026 — one of the largest in the company's ninety-seven-year history — represents a direct investment in expanding and deepening its geological knowledge base. The bulk of the allocation is directed toward Palmarejo, where continued East Corridor drilling aims to convert inferred resources at San Miguel, La Union, and Independencia Sur to the measured and indicated categories required for mine-plan incorporation, and toward New Afton, where K-Zone definition drilling and geomechanical studies will advance the block-cave feasibility work. Las Chispas and the Silvertip polymetallic project in northern British Columbia receive secondary allocations. In a sector where the IP that matters cannot be filed or registered, the exploration budget is as close as mining gets to an R&D line — and the returns, measured in resource additions and mine-life extension, are ultimately what determine whether the geological moat deepens or erodes.

chapters.title: Six Risks That Could Unmake the Transformation Thesis
chapters.body:
## The Price of Ambition

Every transformation story carries within it the seeds of its own reversal. Coeur Mining's reinvention — from overleveraged Idaho silver miner to seven-mine North American conglomerate — was assembled through a sequence of improbable execution wins: the Rochester POA 11 ramp, the Las Chispas integration, the rapid balance-sheet repair. By May 2026, the market had repriced CDE shares from roughly $4 to $18.34, awarding Mitchell Krebs's decade of restructuring with a market capitalisation of approximately $18.8 billion. What follows is an accounting of the six structural risks that could unwind that repricing — not tail risks, but identifiable, recurring categories of failure that have claimed comparable mining transformations before.

---

## Risk 1 — New Gold Integration: Two Mines With Long Memories of Disappointment

The $7 billion all-stock New Gold acquisition, which closed on March 20, 2026, added Rainy River and New Afton to a company that had never before operated in Canada. Both assets carry operational histories that predate Coeur's ownership — and those histories are instructive.

Rainy River, located in northwestern Ontario, was developed by New Gold at capital costs that persistently overran initial estimates, a pattern common to remote Canadian open-pit projects with variable ore bodies and winter-constrained logistics. Mine-plan revisions under prior New Gold management adjusted throughput assumptions, grade expectations, and strip ratios on multiple occasions, each revision compressing the asset's economic contribution relative to original acquisition-case projections. Coeur's 2026 production guidance attributes approximately 245,000–265,000 gold-equivalent ounces to Rainy River — but sustaining that range requires the mine to execute on a sequencing plan it has historically struggled to hold. Any further deviation in grade reconciliation or waste tonnage would erode the asset's free cash flow contribution during what is already the most capital-intensive integration period in Coeur's history.

New Afton presents a different category of risk: technical complexity rather than plan execution. The mine's current operating infrastructure exploits the B-Zone, a mature block-cave near Kamloops, British Columbia. The long-term value thesis rests on the K-Zone, a deeper resource extension that requires new shaft sinking, cave initiation, and sustaining capital over a multi-year development horizon. Block-cave mining — a method that relies on controlled rock fragmentation under gravity — is among the most technically demanding underground disciplines in the industry. Cost overruns and timeline slippage in cave-initiation programs are the norm, not the exception, across the peer set. For Coeur, a company whose underground experience has been concentrated in narrow-vein Mexican silver mines and a conventional gold operation in Alaska, the New Afton K-Zone represents a materially different operational competency requirement. Management has not yet publicly disclosed a detailed capital estimate or development schedule for the K-Zone at the frozen snapshot date, which itself signals the degree of uncertainty embedded in the asset.

---

## Risk 2 — Commodity Price Reversal: A $3 Billion Earnings Estimate Built on $4,550 Gold

Coeur's 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of approximately $3 billion is calculated at gold of $4,550 per ounce and silver of $77.50 per ounce — prices that, as of the frozen snapshot date, reflect a genuine market environment but sit well above any long-run consensus. Both metals remain subject to reversal catalysts that operate independently of Coeur's operational performance: Federal Reserve policy normalization, a return of dollar strength, demand destruction from slowing industrial activity, or the disinflation of safe-haven premia that accumulated during the 2024–2025 macro uncertainty cycle.

A reversion scenario to $3,000 per ounce gold and $30 per ounce silver — levels that prevailed as recently as mid-2024 — would not merely trim Coeur's margins. It would collapse free cash flow toward breakeven on the current cost structure, and potentially re-trigger balance-sheet stress given $300 million of remaining debt and annual sustaining capital requirements of approximately $200 million or more across seven mines. The company's $400–500 million cash tax obligation for 2026, sized to current spot-price profitability, would become a severe liquidity drain in a price-decline scenario if tax installment payments were not rapidly adjusted.

The arithmetic is stark: Coeur's 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 billion was generated with silver averaging well below $77.50 and gold below $4,550. The gap between 2025 actuals and 2026 guidance is substantially attributable to price appreciation, not operational improvement. This makes the consolidated earnings power far more sensitive to commodity price than the headline transformation narrative suggests.

---

## Risk 3 — Mexico Geopolitical and Regulatory Concentration

Las Chispas and Palmarejo, Coeur's two highest-margin silver assets, are both located in Mexico — a jurisdiction that has grown materially more complex for foreign mining operators since 2020. The AMLO administration's 2022 constitutional reform to prioritise state-owned Pemex and CFE energy resources created a legal framework under which mining concessions could be challenged on water-use and environmental grounds with limited foreign-investor recourse. The Claudia Sheinbaum administration, which took office in October 2024, has signalled continuity with the broad thrust of resource nationalism, and pending legislation on mining-concession renewals remained unresolved as of the frozen snapshot date.

Beyond regulatory risk, Sonora state — where Las Chispas operates in Arizpe Municipality — has experienced documented cartel-related security incidents affecting other mining operators. Extortion demands, road blockades, and community-relation disputes have disrupted operations at comparable Sonoran properties in the 2022–2025 period. Coeur has not disclosed specific security incidents at Las Chispas, but the risk is not hypothetical: it represents a recurring operating cost and continuity vulnerability that is structurally absent at the company's US and Canadian mines.

Collectively, the two Mexican mines contribute a disproportionate share of Coeur's EBITDA margin given their high-grade, low-cost profiles. Any regulatory curtailment, permitting delay, or security-driven operating interruption in Mexico would have an outsized impact on consolidated earnings relative to the assets' share of production volume.

---

## Risk 4 — The Franco-Nevada Stream: Structural Revenue Foregone, Permanently

The gold streaming agreement with Franco-Nevada at Palmarejo — under which approximately 40–50 percent of annual gold production is delivered at a fixed price of $800 per ounce — is among the most consequential legacy obligations in Coeur's capital structure. At current spot gold prices near $4,550 per ounce, the annual revenue foregone on the streamed portion is estimated at $150–185 million. The obligation is long-dated, with no scheduled termination visible in public disclosures as of the frozen snapshot date.

Management's stated mitigation strategy is to concentrate exploration capital at Palmarejo on areas of the property that lie outside the stream-affected footprint, theoretically growing the non-streamed share of gold production over time. This is a reasonable incremental approach, but it will not materially alter the economics of the existing streaming obligation within any investment-horizon relevant to current shareholders. At $4,550/oz gold, $150 million of annually foregone revenue represents more than five percentage points of margin compression on the consolidated revenue base — a permanent tax on the asset's earnings power that would have been far more tolerable at $1,500/oz gold.

---

## Risk 5 — Las Chispas Cost Creep: The Premium Asset at Risk of Commoditisation

Las Chispas was acquired in February 2025 precisely because SilverCrest Metals had demonstrated the ability to operate it at sub-$10 per silver ounce all-in sustaining costs as a single-asset, owner-managed operator. That cost position was exceptional in the global silver mining context and formed the primary valuation justification for the $1.7 billion transaction.

The early integration data is less encouraging than the deal thesis assumed. Las Chispas reported adjusted cash costs of $10.75 per silver ounce in Q3 2025, and on a full-year 2025 basis the mine recorded $19.11 per silver ounce when corporate overhead allocations were included. The divergence between the two figures — $10.75 on a direct-cost basis versus $19.11 all-in — reflects the corporate overhead burden that comes with embedding a single-asset mine inside a seven-mine conglomerate: shared IT systems, consolidated insurance, expanded legal and compliance functions, and incremental management layers that did not exist when SilverCrest ran the asset alone.

The risk is not that Las Chispas becomes a bad mine. The ore grades remain exceptional. The risk is that Coeur's administrative superstructure permanently inflates the asset's cost position to a level that narrows the competitive advantage that justified the acquisition premium. If direct operating costs also drift upward as local labour markets tighten in Sonora or maintenance cycles lengthen under a more distributed management structure, the gap between Las Chispas and a generic high-quality silver mine will compress in ways that the acquisition price did not anticipate.

---

## Risk 6 — The Dilution Treadmill and the Per-Share Value Problem

Coeur's share count stood at approximately 399 million at year-end 2024. After the SilverCrest close in February 2025 it expanded to approximately 642 million. After the New Gold acquisition closed in March 2026 it reached approximately 1.03 billion — a 2.6x increase in under 18 months.

The company's ability to generate genuine shareholder value now depends entirely on per-share metrics, not absolute figures. A company that doubles its EBITDA while tripling its share count has not created value for existing shareholders; it has merely redistributed the same economic pie across a larger number of claims. Coeur's 2026 EBITDA guidance of $3 billion implies approximately $2.91 per share — a figure that would need to grow materially over successive years to justify the current share price of $18.34 at any reasonable earnings multiple.

If Rainy River underperforms its acquisition-case production assumptions, or if New Afton's K-Zone development slips by two years, or if Las Chispas costs continue to drift — under any of those scenarios, diluted earnings per share could stagnate or decline even as the company reports record absolute EBITDA. This is the dilution treadmill: the structural challenge of a serial acquirer that must compound per-share earnings rather than just aggregate earnings to sustain its market capitalisation. It is a challenge that Kinross Gold, Pan American Silver, and Hecla Mining have each navigated with mixed results across comparable expansion cycles — and it remains Coeur's most consequential open question as the transformation thesis enters its most complex operational phase.

chapters.title: 2026–2030: The Post-Integration Thesis and the Case for Per-Share Value Creation
chapters.body:
## The Numbers Behind the Narrative

By the spring of 2026, Coeur Mining had assembled a production and financial profile that would have been unrecognisable to the board that convened in Chicago five years earlier to approve the Rochester POA 11 capital programme. Management's 2026 full-year guidance — issued in conjunction with the Q1 2026 results and premised on gold at $4,550 per ounce and silver at $77.50 per ounce — called for 680,000 to 815,000 gold ounces, 18.7 to 21.9 million silver ounces, and 50 to 65 million copper pounds, translating to approximately $3 billion of adjusted EBITDA and $2 billion of free cash flow. Capital expenditure was guided at $305 to $364 million, exploration investment at $120 to $136 million, and cash taxes at $400 to $500 million — the last figure alone a testament to how far the company had travelled from the era of net operating loss carryforwards and covenant waivers. These are management estimates, not writer projections, and they embed commodity price assumptions well above ten-year historical averages; but even discounted modestly, the arithmetic describes a company generating more free cash flow in a single year than its entire market capitalisation commanded in early 2023.

The critical question facing investors at the frozen snapshot date was not whether Coeur had become large. It had. The question was whether the per-share economics would compound from here — or whether a share count of approximately 1.03 billion, more than 2.5 times the pre-SilverCrest level, had permanently diluted the equity's leverage to the underlying asset quality.

## The Three Integration Tests That Will Decide the Decade

Three concurrent integration milestones, each carrying materially different risk profiles, will determine whether the 2025–2026 acquisition sequence creates or erodes shareholder value over the medium term.

The first, and most granular, is the sustained cost performance at Las Chispas. SilverCrest Metals operated the mine at adjusted costs below $10 per silver ounce as a focused single-asset developer; by Q3 2025, the first full quarter under Coeur ownership, costs had risen to $10.75 per ounce, and the full-year 2025 blended figure of $19.11 reflected a partial-year effect including startup and integration overhead. Management has attributed the variance partly to the short initial contribution period and partially to integration costs that are expected to dissipate. If Las Chispas settles sustainably below $15 per silver ounce — the threshold management has implicitly referenced as the post-integration normalised range — it remains among the handful of globally competitive silver mines capable of generating strong margins across commodity cycles. If corporate overhead, expanded workforce costs, or declining head grades push the figure structurally above that level, the $1.7 billion SilverCrest acquisition premium will have been partially consumed by the integration process rather than accreted to shareholders.

The second test is the New Gold operational dossier. Rainy River, the Ontario gold mine added via the March 2026 close, carries the most immediate execution risk: its mine plan requires a near-term update, and confirmation of sustaining capital guidance will be the first real indication of whether Coeur inherited an operationally stable asset or a capital-absorption risk. New Afton, the British Columbia block-cave, presents a longer-dated but strategically significant decision point — the K-Zone resource extension, which would materially extend the mine's productive life, requires a development commitment whose timeline and capital intensity had not been fully disclosed as of the frozen snapshot date. A positive K-Zone decision, if accompanied by credible cost estimates and a defined payback period, would transform New Afton from a cash-flowing asset with a visible decline curve into a decade-scale production anchor.

The third test is the Rochester throughput ramp. By year-end 2025, Rochester had produced 6.1 million silver ounces and 60,178 gold ounces at an adjusted cost of $18.39 per silver ounce — progress against the steep ramp of 2024, but still well short of the economics that would justify $730 million of capital at sustaining-level returns. The 2027–2028 thesis for Rochester is specific: if the mine reaches 32 million tonnes of annual ore throughput at improving Merrill-Crowe recovery rates, management and independent analysts have suggested that adjusted cash costs could decline toward $14 to $16 per silver ounce, potentially transforming Rochester into one of the largest-volume, structurally competitive heap-leach silver producers in North America. The original POA 11 investment thesis was predicated on exactly this outcome — a volume-driven cost curve break. The timeline has slipped two to three years from initial projections, but the mechanical rationale remains intact. Throughput metrics at Rochester in 2026 and 2027 will be the clearest leading indicator of whether the original thesis will ultimately be vindicated.

## Allocating the Cash: Debt, Dividends, Buybacks, and the M&A Question

The $2 billion of guided 2026 free cash flow poses an allocation question that Coeur's management team has not faced before. After meeting the $400 to $500 million cash tax obligation and funding $305 to $364 million of sustaining and development capital, the residual cash flow will encounter competing claims.

Further debt reduction would be accretive to financial flexibility — the remaining debt on the balance sheet as of year-end 2025 was only $341 million against $554 million of cash, implying a net cash position even before 2026 generation — but with leverage already at historically low levels, the marginal risk-reduction benefit of additional debt paydown is diminishing. The inaugural semi-annual dividend of $0.02 per share, declared in May 2026, signals intent but represents a negligible yield at current share prices; meaningful dividend growth, while symbolically important, would consume a modest portion of available capital at the scale required to be competitively yielded against streaming-company peers. Share buybacks present a more mathematically potent lever: at 1.03 billion shares and a market price near $18.34, a $500 million buyback programme would retire approximately 2.7 percent of the share count, meaningfully offsetting the share dilution creep that has persistently weighed on per-share metrics through the acquisition cycle.

The M&A question is the one management has most conspicuously declined to foreclose. Krebs has built a career on transaction-driven portfolio construction, and the pattern of opportunistic acquisition — Wharf, then Rochester expansion, then Las Chispas, then New Gold — suggests a continued appetite for consolidation. The Silvertip polymetallic exploration project in northern British Columbia, held but undeveloped, represents one organic option for internal capital deployment. A further acquisition in the current precious metals price environment, however, would risk the per-share dilution narrative precisely when the market is watching for its reversal.

## Palmarejo's Quiet Revaluation

One underappreciated element of the medium-term case is the exploration programme at Palmarejo. A 36 to 40 percent increase in gold and silver reserves at year-end 2025, achieved through drilling in areas outside the Franco-Nevada stream-affected zone, represents a potential multi-year value catalyst. The Franco-Nevada gold stream — which entitles the royalty company to approximately 40 to 50 percent of Palmarejo's annual gold production at a fixed $800 per ounce — has been a structural drag on the mine's revenue realisation since the stream was established. New discoveries outside the stream's contractual perimeter do not fall within the stream's delivery obligations, meaning that reserve growth in those zones would generate revenue at full spot prices rather than the $800 fixed rate. If the 2026 to 2028 drilling programme continues to delineate reserve additions in stream-exempt areas, the proportional revenue burden of the stream will decline as a percentage of total Palmarejo output — a genuine structural improvement in the mine's economics, achieved without renegotiating or paying down the stream.

## The Five-Year Thesis: Bull Case and Bear Case

The base case thesis for Coeur through 2030 rests on four compounding assumptions: that Las Chispas sustains costs below $15 per silver ounce; that Rochester achieves its 32 million tonne throughput target by 2028; that Rainy River and New Afton deliver at or above the production and cost guidance embedded in the New Gold acquisition model; and that precious metals prices remain sufficiently elevated to generate free cash flow margins in the 65 to 70 percent range. On these assumptions, a company producing approximately 750,000 gold ounces and 20 million silver ounces annually, with an $18 to $20 billion market capitalisation and a demonstrated track record of converting acquired assets into operating success, would represent a genuinely differentiated position in the North American precious-metals landscape — a company with the production scale of a senior miner, the cost structure of a portfolio operator, and the exploration optionality of a junior.

The bear case is structurally symmetric. New Gold integration falters: Rainy River's mine plan requires a capital-intensive revision that erodes free cash flow in 2027 and 2028, New Afton's K-Zone development encounters technical delays, and Las Chispas cost creep proves structural rather than transitional. Commodity prices retrace toward historical averages — gold at $2,500 to $3,000 per ounce, silver at $30 to $40 — compressing EBITDA margins and eliminating the cash generation that currently underwrites the capital allocation optionality. In this scenario, a share count of 1.03 billion, a market capitalisation that has priced in substantial execution success, and an operational footprint spanning five jurisdictions and three currencies would leave the company navigating the kind of multi-front stress test that Krebs managed through balance-sheet discipline in 2015 and 2016 — but at a scale, and with a complexity, that has no precedent in the company's history.

The market, at $18.34 per share and approximately 6x 2026 guided EBITDA as of late May 2026, was not yet paying a premium for execution certainty. That premium, or its absence, would be earned or forfeited over the next eight quarters.

## Appendix E: Franco-Nevada Streaming Agreement at Palmarejo — Standing Disclosure

Under the legacy gold streaming agreement governing Palmarejo, [Franco-Nevada](https://www.franco-nevada.com) receives approximately 40–50 percent of Palmarejo's annual underground gold production at a fixed delivery price of $800 per ounce — a price that, against a spot gold price exceeding $4,500 per ounce as of the frozen snapshot date, represents a structurally below-market realisation on a defined tranche of revenue. The agreement materially compresses Palmarejo's net gold revenue and is reflected in the mine's reported adjusted cost metrics. Management's stated long-term response is exploration activity directed outside the stream-affected underground zone, with the objective of identifying satellite deposits or surface resources whose economics are not encumbered by the Franco-Nevada entitlement. Coeur has not disclosed any renegotiation or buy-down of the stream; it is treated as a permanent fixture in the Palmarejo financial model for all guidance periods within the frozen window.

financials.key_finding: Coeur Mining's financial trajectory between 2024 and the frozen snapshot date of May 2026 represents one of the most compressed inflection points in recent North American precious-metals history. Revenue nearly doubled from $1.1 billion in fiscal year 2024 to $2.1 billion in fiscal year 2025, driven by the full-year contribution of the Rochester POA 11 ramp-up, the February 2025 addition of Las Chispas, and a sharp rise in realised silver and gold prices. Net income swung from $59 million in 2024 to $586 million in 2025, and adjusted EBITDA tripled from $339 million to $1.0 billion. Free cash flow moved from negative $9 million in 2024 to positive $666 million in 2025 — a $675 million swing that funded $249 million of debt repayment and left the company with $554 million of cash at year-end 2025. Total debt fell 42 percent to $341 million, and the net leverage ratio declined from approximately 1.7x at year-end 2024 to well below 1.0x by mid-2025. The Q1 2026 quarter, which included only eleven days of New Gold contribution following the March 20, 2026 close, reported record revenue of $856 million and adjusted EBITDA of $475 million — a quarterly EBITDA run rate that, if sustained, implies approximately $1.9 billion of full-year EBITDA on the legacy five-mine portfolio alone, before the full-year New Gold impact. Management's 2026 full-year guidance assumes gold at $4,550/oz and silver at $77.50/oz and projects consolidated EBITDA of roughly $3 billion with free cash flow of approximately $2 billion. Capital expenditure guidance for 2026 is $305–364 million (sustaining plus development), with exploration investment of $120–136 million. Cash taxes are expected to be $400–500 million, reflecting the heavily profitable operating environment. The capital structure as of the frozen snapshot date is characterised by substantial equity dilution from the two all-stock acquisitions — shares outstanding expanded from approximately 399 million at year-end 2024 to approximately 642 million after the SilverCrest close and further to approximately 1.03 billion after New Gold — combined with disciplined debt management that has kept leverage well below the levels that threatened the company's viability during the 2013–2016 silver price downturn. The market capitalisation of approximately $18.8 billion at $18.34 per share as of May 26, 2026 implies an EV/EBITDA multiple of approximately 6x on the 2026 guided EBITDA — a discount to streaming peers (Franco-Nevada, Royal Gold, Wheaton Precious Metals) but broadly in line with producing-miner peers such as Pan American Silver, First Majestic, and Hecla Mining.
structural_observations: Revenue base quadrupled in two years: from approximately $510 million in 2023 to approximately $1.1 billion in 2024 and approximately $2.1 billion in 2025, driven by Rochester POA 11 throughput ramp, Las Chispas addition in February 2025, and silver/gold price appreciation; Q1 2026 revenue of $856 million annualises to over $3.4 billion with full New Gold contribution.

Fiscal year cadence is calendar-year (January–December) with quarterly 10-Q filings; the company reports five operating segments — Las Chispas, Palmarejo, Rochester, Kensington, Wharf — as of fiscal year 2025, to be expanded to seven segments (adding Rainy River and New Afton) starting with Q1 2026 10-Q disclosure.

Margin progression has been dramatic but uneven across mines: Las Chispas carries the portfolio's best margins (adjusted EBITDA margin near 70 percent), Palmarejo and Wharf are mid-tier performers (adjusted costs $871/oz Au and $1,151/oz Au respectively), while Rochester ($18.39/oz Ag adjusted CAS in 2025) and Kensington ($1,685/oz Au adjusted CAS) compress consolidated margins; the Franco-Nevada gold stream at Palmarejo imposes a structural cost discount on approximately 40–50 percent of that mine's gold revenue.

Capital structure transformed: total debt of $341 million as of December 31, 2025 against cash of $554 million implies a net cash position; however, the New Gold acquisition was all-stock, so balance sheet leverage is modest while dilution is substantial — shares outstanding grew from 399 million (year-end 2024) to approximately 1.03 billion (post-New Gold, May 2026), a 2.6x increase in less than 18 months.

Debt composition: remaining debt consists primarily of senior secured notes and drawn revolving credit facility balances; the company has been amortising the balance aggressively (year-to-date debt repayment exceeded $228 million through Q3 2025) and targets continued deleveraging; the 2026 cash tax obligation of $400–500 million is the largest single cash outflow claim on free cash flow.

Comparable peers by market cap and operating profile include Pan American Silver (PAAS), First Majestic Silver (AG), Hecla Mining (HL), and Endeavour Silver (EXK) on the silver-weighted side; for diversified North American gold-silver producers, Kinross Gold (KGC) and Iamgold (IAG) offer valuation reference points; Coeur's market cap of approximately $18.8 billion by May 2026 places it well above prior-year peer groupings and closer to Kinross territory.

Market cap volatility has been extreme: CDE shares traded near $4–5 in 2023 during the Rochester capital peak and balance sheet stress, rose to approximately $9–10 post-Las Chispas close in early 2025, and had reached approximately $18 by mid-May 2026, implying roughly a 3.5x increase over an 18-month window driven by the simultaneous inflection of operational execution, acquired asset performance, and precious metals price appreciation.

leadership.key_finding: Mitchell J. Krebs has served as President and Chief Executive Officer of Coeur Mining since 2011, making him one of the longest-tenured CEOs among US-listed precious-metals producers. He joined the company in 1995 — then still Coeur d'Alene Mines — as a junior corporate development professional after beginning his career in investment banking in New York. He worked through a sequence of corporate development roles, reaching Senior Vice President before his elevation to CEO. Krebs's educational background (Wharton undergraduate, Harvard MBA) is atypical for a mining CEO and reflects his orientation toward capital allocation and transaction structuring rather than operational geology. His tenure spans the company's most critical strategic transitions: the 2013 Idaho-to-Chicago headquarters relocation and corporate rebrand; balance-sheet rehabilitation after the 2015–2016 commodity price collapse, which required aggressive cost-cutting and asset sales; the multi-year commitment to the Rochester POA 11 expansion, which consumed $730 million of capital; and the two major acquisitions of 2024–2026 (SilverCrest/Las Chispas and New Gold). CFO Thomas S. Whelan joined in 2019 from Arizona Mining, where he also served as CFO; his background spans accounting, capital markets, and risk management in the metals and mining sector, and he has been the architect of Coeur's rapid 2025 deleveraging. The board of directors, led by independent Chairman Robert E. Mellor, comprises nine directors; a proxy filed in early 2025 noted four new directors added in the preceding three years as part of active board refreshment. Rob Krcmarov was appointed to the board in December 2023, adding deep operational mining expertise. The 2025 Annual Incentive Plan paid out at 133 percent of target and the Long-Term Incentive Plan paid out at 166 percent of target, both reflecting the strong operational and financial performance of the year. The company received greater than 97 percent shareholder support on its 2025 say-on-pay vote. There is no private equity sponsor or activist presence; Coeur is an entirely publicly owned company with no controlling shareholder block.
research_notes_for_writer: Verify whether Mitchell Krebs received any equity grants or retention arrangements tied to the SilverCrest or New Gold transactions; the DEF 14A proxy at https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000215466/000114036125011870/ny20041389x1_def14a.htm contains the compensation tables — check for one-time transaction bonuses or accelerated vesting provisions.

Identify all current board directors by name and committee assignment: the 2025 proxy lists nine directors including the independent chairman; confirm whether any SilverCrest or New Gold directors were added to the board post-close, which would be disclosed in 8-K filings around February 2025 and March 2026.

CFO Thomas Whelan's tenure at Arizona Mining is relevant because Arizona Mining was a silver-zinc developer acquired by South32 in 2018 — his experience with a single-project developer versus a multi-asset producer is worth contextualising for the chapter on financial strategy; confirm current LTIP vesting schedule and any retention risk.

Investigate the Kansas City Southern Railway board connection for Mitchell Krebs — that company was acquired by Canadian Pacific in 2023 to form CPKC; determine whether Krebs remained on the combined CPKC board and what this says about his external network and time demands.

Rob Krcmarov was previously Chief Exploration Officer at Barrick Gold; his December 2023 appointment to the Coeur board is likely connected to the company's exploration-led reserve growth strategy at Palmarejo and Kensington — explore whether he has played a role in shaping the exploration investment budget that reached $120–136 million in 2026 guidance.

Determine whether the New Gold transaction brought any former New Gold executives into Coeur's leadership team; New Gold's former President and CEO Renaud Adams has a strong reputation in the mining industry, and his disposition post-close (retained, departed, or advisory) is material to understanding integration governance.

Assess internal succession depth: Krebs has been CEO for 15 years as of 2026; the proxy should list other Section 16 officers including the COO or Chief Operating Officer equivalent, VP Operations, and Chief Sustainability Officer — identifying this bench is important for long-form dossier readers evaluating key-person risk.
